Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:07:44.909+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Court Gentleman for Closing Court, Right Rectifier of Omissions, Acting Palace Censor, Concurrently Commissioner of the Bureau of Review, Commandant of the Upper Guards, Granted the Purple and Gold Fish Pouch, Your Subject
Feng Chi Compiled
Later Student Tiāntāi
Lù Démíng said: Qín,
is the name of a valley in Lǒngxī,
located northeast of Wūshǔ Mountain in Yōngzhōu.
The ancestor of Qín, Fēizǐ,
raised horses for King Xiào of Zhōu between the Qiān and Wèi rivers,
and was enfeoffed as an attached vassal,
with his domain at Qíngǔ.
Fēizǐ’s great-grandson, Qín Zhòng,
was appointed as a Grand Master by King Xuān of Zhōu.
Zhòng’s grandson, Duke Xiāng,
attacked the Western Róng and rescued Zhōu.
When King Píng moved east,
he granted him the lands of Qí and Fēng,
ranking him among the feudal lords.
During the Spring and Autumn period, he was called the Earl of Qín.
King Zhāoxiāng
named Jì,
was a son of King Huiwén by a concubine.
After Western Zhōu perished,
no one in the world was fit to be the ruler.
The Comprehensive Mirror, because Qín ultimately unified the world,
thus used King Zhāoxiāng to mark the years.
The rules of posthumous naming: “Having illustrious virtue and toil is called Zhāo”;
“Expanding territory with virtue is called Xiāng.”
According to Shěn Yuē’s rules of posthumous naming,
then Zhāoxiāng is a double posthumous name.
Zú,
zǐ xù fān.
Shì,
shén zhì fān.
Pì,
dú yuē pì.
1 The Governor of Hédōng, Wáng Jī, was implicated in communicating with the feudal lords,
and was executed in the marketplace.
Hédōng was originally territory of Wèi,
which Qín seized.
Because the land was east of the great river,
they established Hédōng Commandery.
Shǒu,
shì yòu fān.
Executing a person in the marketplace,
means discarding him together with the masses.
Under Qín law, those sentenced to death were executed in the marketplace,
called “discarding in the marketplace.”
Wáng Jī recommended Fàn Suī to the King of Qín.
After Suī became Chancellor of Qín,
Jī was also promoted and employed.
Now he died for his crime,
so Suī grew increasingly unhappy.
Yì,
means pleased.
Bù yì,
means not pleased.
Yìng,
yú líng fān.
Some say: When Fàn Suī was first employed in Qín,
up to becoming chancellor,
King Zhāoxiāng truly delighted in him.
After Zhèng Ānpíng surrendered to Zhào,
and Wáng Jī was found guilty,
although Suī was chancellor,
when King Zhāoxiāng held court and received him,
he grew increasingly displeased.
Yì,
yáng yì fān.
Marquis Yìng asked the reason.
The King said:
“Now that Lord Wǔ’ān is dead,
and Zhèng Ānpíng, Wáng Jī, and others have all rebelled,
within we lack good generals, and without we have many enemy states.
This is why I worry!”
Marquis Yīng was afraid,
and did not know what to do.
A guest from Yān, Cài Zé, heard of this,
and went west to enter Qín.
First, he sent someone to declare to Marquis Yīng:
“Cài Zé
is a powerfully eloquent scholar of the world.
When he sees the King,
he will surely corner you and seize your position.”
Marquis Yīng was angry,
and sent someone to summon him.
When Cài Zé met Marquis Yīng,
his demeanor was also arrogant.
Marquis Yīng was displeased,
and thus reproached him, saying:
“You declared you want to replace me as chancellor.
I ask to hear your reasoning.”
Cài Zé said:
“Alas,
Kǒng Ānguó said: Alas,
is an expression of doubt and wonder.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: ‘Alas’
is uttered when the heart harbors suspicion,
thus it is considered an expression of doubt and wonder.
Now the sequence of the four seasons
is that when one completes its task, it departs.
That is to say, spring gives birth,
summer grows,
autumn bears fruit,
winter closes and stores,
each completes its task and they succeed one another.
Fú,
yīn fú;
xià tóng.
Why should one cling to it?”
For the affairs of Lord Shāng, see the thirty-first year of King Xiǎn of Zhōu in the second scroll.
For the affairs of Wú Qǐ, see the twenty-first year of King Ān in the first scroll.
Grand Master Zhǒng served King Gōujiàn of Yuè to wipe out the shame of Kuàijī.
When his task was accomplished, he did not withdraw,
and was killed by Gōujiàn.
Zhǒng,
Wēn Gōng yīn zhāng yǒng fān.
Yǔ,
dú yuē yú.
Gōu,
yīn gōu.
Jiàn,
cí qiǎn fān.
Zhǒng,
zhāng yǒng fān.
“Why is it not possible!
These three gentlemen
reached the utmost in righteousness,
and exhausted loyalty.
A gentleman may sacrifice his life to establish his name,
and die without regret.”
Cài Zé said:
“When a person achieves merit,
does he not hope for complete success?
When both body and name are preserved, that is
the best;
when the name is exemplary but the body dies, that is
the next best;
when the name is disgraced but the body is preserved, that is
the worst.
Lù,
is the same as lù.
As a subject, to exhaust loyalty and achieve merit
is indeed desirable.
Hóng Yāo and the Duke of Zhōu,
were they not also loyal and sagely?
Compared to Hóng Yāo and the Duke of Zhōu,
how do the three gentlemen measure up?”
Hóng Yāo
was a worthy minister of King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu.
Hóng,
yīn hóng.
Yāo,
yú jiāo fān,
yòu yú biǎo fān.
“Well said.”
Cài Zé said:
“Then, in terms of your lord’s kindness and faithfulness to old acquaintances,
and not betraying meritorious ministers,
how does he compare to Duke Xiào, the King of Chǔ, and the King of Yuè?”
He said:
“I do not know how they compare.”
Cài Zé said:
“How does your merit and ability compare to the three gentlemen?”
He said:
“I am not as good.”
Cài Zé said:
“Then if you do not withdraw from your position,
your calamity may be greater than that of the three gentlemen.
As the saying goes: ‘When the sun reaches its zenith, it shifts;
when the moon is full, it wanes.’
Advancing and retreating, expanding and contracting,
the five planets appearing early is called expansion,
appearing late is called contraction.
Yíng,
yú qīng fān.
Suō,
suǒ liù fān.
This is the way of the sage.
Now your grievances have been avenged and your kindness repaid.
Grievances avenged
refers to killing Wèi Qí;
kindness repaid
refers to promoting and employing Wáng Jī, Zhèng Ānpíng, and others.
I privately worry for your danger!”
Marquis Yīng then invited him as a guest of honor,
and recommended him to the King.
The King summoned him and spoke with him,
was greatly pleased,
and appointed him as a guest minister.
Marquis Yīng then pleaded illness and resigned.
The King, newly pleased with Cài Zé’s plans,
then made him Chancellor of State.
Zé served as chancellor for several months,
and was dismissed.
2. Chǔ’s Lord Chūnshēn appointed Xún Qīng as the Magistrate of Lánlíng.
The Xìng Pǔ states: The surname Xún
originally came from the surname Huán.
Later, the
“yì” radical
was removed,
becoming “Xún.”
Also, Xún Línfǔ of Jìn
was a descendant of the ducal clan’s Xí Shū.
According to the Bǎn Zhì,
Lánlíng County belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: In present-day Yízhōu, Chéng County has Lánlíng Mountain.
He was a man of Zhào,
named Kuàng,
who once debated military affairs with Lord Línwǔ before King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
The King said:
“May I ask about the essentials of warfare?”
Lord Línwǔ replied:
“Above, one must grasp the opportune time;
below, one must secure advantageous terrain;
observe the enemy’s movements;
strike after them,
yet arrive before them.
These are the essential techniques of employing troops.”
“After” and “before”
are both read in the falling tone.
“Not so.
What I have heard of the ancient way
is that the foundation of all military campaigns
lies in unifying the people.
If the bow and arrows are not properly adjusted,
even Yì could not hit the target;
if the six horses are not in harmony,
even Zàofù could not travel far.
Yì
was an expert archer of antiquity;
Zàofù
was an expert charioteer of antiquity.
Yì
is pronounced yì.
“Hit”
is pronounced zhòng.
“Fù”
is pronounced fǔ.
Then even Tāng and Wǔ could not be certain of victory.
Therefore, one who excels at winning over the people
is truly one who excels at employing troops.
Thus, the essential of warfare lies solely in winning over the people.”
Lord Línwǔ said:
“Not so.
What is valued in warfare is momentum and advantage;
what is practiced is deception and cunning.
Those skilled in employing troops act swiftly and unpredictably,
Yáng Jìng said: ‘Gǎnhū’ means indistinct,
vague.
‘Yōu’àn’
refers to a distant, unclear appearance.
Sūn and Wú used these methods,
becoming invincible under heaven.
How could they necessarily rely on winning over the people?”
Xún Qīng said:
“Not so.
What I speak of
is the army of a benevolent person,
the ambition of a true king.
What you value,
is tactical schemes, momentum, and advantage.
The army of a benevolent person
cannot be deceived.
Those who can be deceived
are the negligent and careless,
the exposed and uncovered.
‘Exposed and uncovered’
is like a person whose limbs and body have no clothing to cover them,
bare and naked.
Thus, for a Jié to deceive another Jié,
there may still be a chance of skill versus clumsiness.
For a Jié to deceive a Yáo,
is like throwing an egg at a stone,
poking boiling water with a finger,
or rushing into water or fire—
entering it, one will be scorched and submerged.
Therefore, the army of a benevolent person
is of one mind from top to bottom,
with all three armies united in strength.
The relationship between minister and ruler,
subordinate and superior,
is like a son serving his father,
a younger brother serving his elder brother,
like arms and hands defending the head and eyes and covering the chest and abdomen.
To deceive and launch a surprise attack,
or to first alarm and then strike—
it is all the same.
Moreover, a benevolent person governing a state of ten lǐ will have intelligence spanning a hundred lǐ;
governing a state of a hundred lǐ will have intelligence spanning a thousand lǐ;
governing a state of a thousand lǐ will have intelligence spanning the four seas.
They will surely be perceptive, vigilant,
harmonious, united, and of one purpose.
Therefore, the army of a benevolent person,
when gathered, forms a zú
(a unit of one hundred men).
When extended, it is like the long blade of Mòyé,
Mòyé
being a treasured sword of Wú.
The Shuōwén states: Mòyé
is a long halberd.
“Yé”
is pronounced yé.
When concentrated, it is like the sharp edge of Mòyé;
those who face it will crumble.
“Duì”
appears as
“ruì”
in Liú Xiàng’s Xīnxù.
Yáng Jìng said: Duì
means to gather,
read the same as duì.
Jìng
is pronounced liàng.
It is like a massive rock;
those who touch it will have their horns broken and retreat.
Furthermore, the rulers of violent states—
with whom will they come?
Those who come with them
must be their own people.
Their people’s affection for me is joyful, like toward parents;
their fondness for me is fragrant, like pepper and orchid.
When they look back at their superiors, it is like being branded or tattooed,
like facing an enemy.
By human nature,
even a Jié or a Zhí—
would they willingly do what they detest
and harm what they love?
Character dictionaries: Chóu and chóu
both mean ‘match.’
The Shuōwén states: Chóu
means ‘enemy.’
Chóu also means ‘to respond.’
The Zuǒzhuàn states: A resentful match is called chóu.
The Record says: One’s father’s enemy
cannot share the same sky.
This refers to the initial matching in chóu.
When a match turns to resentment,
it becomes chóu.
Chóu
means ‘to compare,’
two versions facing each other,

When facing the killer of one’s father,
checking right and wrong,

The meaning of chóuchóu

later generations generally use it in this sense.
“Fondness”

“Do”

“Detest”

They will surely come to inform me—

Therefore, when a benevolent person is employed,
the state grows daily brighter.
Among the feudal lords, those who submit first are secure,
those who submit later are endangered,
those who oppose are diminished,
and those who rebel are destroyed.
The Odes say:
‘King Wǔ set forth his banners,

like a raging fire,

their implementation and use.
"Generally, when a ruler is worthy, his state is well-ordered;

One who exalts ritual and esteems righteousness will have a well-ordered state;
one who neglects ritual and disdains righteousness will have a chaotic state.
A well-ordered state is strong;
a chaotic state is weak.
This is the root of strength and weakness.
If the superiors are worthy of being looked up to, then the subordinates can be used;
if the superiors are not worthy of being looked up to, then the subordinates cannot be used.
If subordinates can be used, the state is strong;
if subordinates cannot be used, the state is weak.
This is the constant pattern of strength and weakness.
The people of Qí

They placed a spear upon it,

They cause them to grow through achievement and reward:

They are all armies that seek rewards and chase profit,

King Xiàochéng and Lord Línwǔ said:
"Excellent.
May we ask about being a general?"
Master Xún said:
"Wisdom is greatest in abandoning doubt;

One desires safety with weightiness,

means坚守 one principle without change.

"I wish to capture Jīng.
(The King's father, King Zhuāngxiāng, had the personal name Chǔ,
therefore Chǔ was referred to as Jīng.)"
Lǐ Xìn said,
"It would require no more than 200,000 men."
The King asked Wáng Jiǎn about this,
Wáng Jiǎn said,
"It cannot be done without 600,000 men."
The King said,
"General Wáng is old,
how timid he is!"
He then sent Lǐ Xìn and Méng Tián to lead 200,000 men to attack Chǔ;
Wáng Jiǎn consequently pleaded illness and retired to Pínyáng.
Wáng Jiǎn
was a man of Pínyáng.
According to the Bǎn Zhì,
Pínyáng County belonged to Jīngzhào,
established by Duke Lì of Qín.
Yìng Shào annotated: The county is located north of the Pín River.
Dù Yòu said: Měiyáng was originally the Hàn Dynasty's Pínyáng County,
its old city is thirty lǐ southwest of the county seat.
Sòng Bái said: It was named after the Pínyáng Mountain within its borders.
1 Wáng Bēn attacked Wèi,
diverting the Hé Gōu canal to flood Dàliáng.
Bǎn Zhì: The Xùnyí County of Chénliú Commandery,
formerly Dàliáng,
was where the Lángtāng River flowed.
The Shuǐ Jīng states: The Qú River originates from the northern Hé of Xíngyáng,
flowing southeast to Xùnyí County.
The annotation says: The First Emperor sent Wáng Bēn to attack Wèi,
who cut the old canal,
diverting the water to flow southeast to flood Dàliáng,
hence it was called the Liáng Gōu.
The city walls collapsed.
King Jiǎ of Wèi surrendered,
was killed,
and Wèi was thus destroyed.
The King sent a messenger to tell the Lord of Ānlíng:
"I wish to exchange five hundred lǐ of land for Ānlíng."
The Lord of Ānlíng said:
"Your Majesty bestows kindness,
exchanging large for small,
I am most fortunate.
However,
I received this land from the former kings of Wèi,
and wish to guard it to the end,
I dare not exchange it!"
The King, considering it righteous, permitted it.
2 Lǐ Xìn attacked Píngyù,
Bǎn Zhì,
Rǔnán Commandery had Píngyù County,
the state of Shěnzǐ during the Spring and Autumn period.
Yù,
pronounced yù,
the Shǐjì Zhèngyì reads it as the common character.
Bǎn Zhì: Rǔnán Commandery had Jìn County.
Yìng Shào said: This is Jìnqiū, the fief of Sūnshū Áo's son;
Emperor Shìzǔ renamed it Gùshǐ.
Xú Guǎng said: Jìn,
is now Gùshǐ Jìnqiū.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Jìn,
is pronounced zǐ rèn fān.
Liú Zhòngféng said: According to later records, the Huáiyáng Kingdom already had Gùshǐ,
this Jìn is likely a separate place.
I say the merging and splitting of commanderies and counties was irregular,
probably Jìn was later merged into Gùshǐ.
Dù Yòu said: Yǐngzhōu governed Rǔyīn County,
which had Jìnqiū,
Méng Tián's attack on Jìn referred to this place.
Xìn also attacked Yānyǐng,
and captured it.
This Yānyǐng is not the former capital Yānyǐng of Chǔ.
The former capital of Chǔ was captured by Bái Qǐ,
and Qín had already established Nán Commandery.
Considering that the capital of Chǔ was Shòuchūn,
and Shòuchūn was called Yǐng,
then before moving the capital from Yǐng to Chén,
they must also have called Chén Yǐng.
Therefore, this Yǐng refers to Chén.
Yān refers to Yānlíng in Yǐngchuān,
which is close to both Píngyù and Chéngfù.
Some say:
"Yānyǐng"
should be
"Yānlíng".
He joined forces with Méng Tián at Chéngfù.
Bǎn Zhì,
Pèi Commandery had Chéngfù County.
Suǒyǐn said: In Rǔnán, it is Jíliángxiāng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì said: It means leading troops to rendezvous at Chéngfù,
which refers to the Fùchéng east of Jiáchéng County in Rǔzhōu.
Kuòdìzhì: Forty lǐ east of Jiáchéng County in Rǔzhōu is the old city of Fùchéng,
which is what Fú Qián called
"Chéngfù,
the northern border of Chǔ"
refers to.
Also, forty-five lǐ northeast of Yè County in Xǔzhōu is another old city of Fùchéng,
which is what Dù Yù called
"Xiāngchéng,
Chéngfù County"
refers to.
These are two cities,
both named Fùchéng,
Fú Qián's Chéngfù is mistaken.
Zuǒzhuàn and Shuǐjīngzhù state: Chǔ fortified Chéngfù,
and had Crown Prince Jiàn reside there.
Shísānzhōuzhì states: The Chéngfù where Crown Prince Jiàn resided,
refers to present-day Bózhōu Chéngfù,
that is correct.
These three theories
concern the name Chéngfù.
Bǎn Zhì states,
Yǐngchuān Fùchéng County, Pèi Commandery Chéngfù County,
according to the county's belonging to a commandery,
their names are distinct.
For three days and three nights without rest,
they heavily defeated Lǐ Xìn,
entered two fortifications,
and killed seven commandants;
these were commandants of commanderies leading troops to attack Chǔ.
Qín's commanderies had a governor,
a commandant,
and an inspector,
however, according to the Qín and Hàn systems,
armies on campaign also had their own commandants.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
The King heard of this,
was greatly angered,
and personally went to Pínyáng to apologize to Wáng Jiǎn, saying:
"I did not use your strategy,
and Lǐ Xìn indeed brought disgrace upon the Qín army.
Although you are ill,
can you bear to abandon me?"
Wáng Jiǎn declined:
"I am ill and cannot command."
The King said:
"Enough,
say no more!"
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"If you must use me,
it cannot be done without 600,000 men!"
The King said:
"I will follow your plan."
Thereupon, Wáng Jiǎn led 600,000 men to attack Chǔ: The King escorted him to Bàshàng,
Yìng Shào said: Bàshàng,
a place name,
located on the Bà River,
thirty lǐ east of Cháng'ān.
The Bà River,
anciently called the Zī River,
was renamed by Duke Mù of Qín.
The King said:
"General, go now,
why worry about poverty?"
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"To be a general for Your Majesty,
even with achievements,
one ultimately may not be enfeoffed as a marquis,
therefore, while Your Majesty still favors me,
I request fields and houses to establish an estate for my descendants."
The King laughed heartily.
After Wáng Jiǎn set out,
upon reaching the pass,
this likely refers to exiting the Wǔ Pass.
Someone said:
"General, your begging is excessive!"
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"Not so.
The King is suspicious by nature and does not trust others,
now he empties the state of its armored troops and entrusts them solely to me.
If I do not extensively request fields and houses to establish an estate for my descendants to demonstrate my steadfastness,
I would instead make the King sit and doubt me."
1 Wáng Jiǎn captured the territory from Chén south to Píngyú.
When the people of Chǔ heard that Wáng Jiǎn was advancing with additional troops,
they mobilized all the soldiers from within the state to resist him;
Wáng Jiǎn fortified his camp and did not engage in battle.
The Chǔ forces repeatedly challenged them to fight,
but he never emerged.
Wáng Jiǎn daily allowed his soldiers to rest and bathe,
and provided them with good food and drink,
comforting and caring for them;
he personally ate the same food as the rank-and-file soldiers.
After a long time,
Wáng Jiǎn sent someone to ask
"Are the troops playing games in the camp?"
The reply was:
"They are currently throwing stones and leaping over distances."
Xú Guǎng said:
"Chāo,"
in one version is written as
"bá."
Péi Yīn said: According to the Hànshū, Gān Yánshòu could throw stones and leap over distances,
surpassing his peers.
Zhāng Yàn said: In Fàn Lǐ's Art of War: "Flying stones weigh twelve catties,
launched by a mechanism,
they travel three hundred paces.
Yánshòu had great strength,
and could throw them by hand.
Bá jù,
is like chāo jù."
Suǒyǐn said: Chāo jù,
is like leaping and jumping.
I say that tóu shí,
means throwing stones at people,
as Qí's Gāo Gù
"picked up stones to throw at people"
exemplifies.
Chāo jù,
is jù yuè,
as Jìn's Wèi Chōu
"jù yuè three hundred times"
exemplifies.
"They are ready for use!"
Since Chǔ could not engage in battle,
they withdrew eastward.
Wáng Jiǎn pursued them,
ordering his strong warriors to attack,
and heavily defeated the Chǔ army,
reaching south of Qí.
Bān Zhì states,
Pèi Commandery had Qí County.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: It is a county in Xúzhōu.
Kāng believed it was Qíchūn in Jiāngxià,
which is a great error.
Qí,
is pronounced qí zhī fān,
also pronounced jī.
Xiàng Yān,
was the father of Xiàng Liáng.
Yān,
is pronounced wū xián fān.
Wáng Jiǎn then took advantage of the victory to capture and pacify cities and towns.
1 Wáng Jiǎn and Méng Wǔ captured the King of Chǔ, Fù Chú,
and established a Chǔ Commandery over his territory.
Thus, Chǔ perished at this point.
According to the thirty-six commanderies of Qín, there was no Chǔ Commandery,
this was likely temporarily established upon the destruction of Chǔ;
later it was divided into the three commanderies of Jiǔjiāng, Zhāng, and Kuàijī.
1 A great mobilization of troops was ordered,
sending Wáng Bēn to attack Liáodōng,
where he captured the King of Yān, Xǐ.
Thus, Yān perished.
Your subject Guāng remarks: Yān Dān, unable to endure a moment's anger, provoked the tiger-and-wolf-like state of Qín,
with shallow consideration and poor planning,
inciting resentment and hastening disaster,
causing the temple of Shào Gōng to abruptly cease its sacrifices,
hū zhū,
means suddenly perishing.
Yet some commentators consider him worthy,
is that not mistaken indeed!
Those who govern a state,
appoint officials based on talent,
establish governance based on ritual,
win over the people with benevolence,
and interact with neighboring states with good faith;
thus, offices are filled with suitable men,
governance attains proper measure,
the common people cherish their virtue,
and the neighboring states are drawn to their righteousness.
If it is thus,
then the state will be as secure as a rock,
as blazing as a fierce fire,
those who touch it will be shattered,
those who offend it will be scorched.
Even if there are violent and powerful states,
what is there to fear!
Dān abandoned this path,
and instead, with a state of ten thousand chariots,
acted on the anger of a common man,
indulged in the schemes of bandits and thieves,
his achievements ruined and himself executed,
the altars of soil and grain reduced to ruins,
is that not tragic indeed!
Kneeling and crawling on the ground,
is not respect;
keeping one's word and honoring promises,
is not good faith;
fù yán,
means speaking with certainty and being reliable.
Zhòng nuò,
means valuing promises made.
Squandering gold and scattering jade,
is not generosity;
cutting off heads and slitting bellies,
is not courage.
In summary,
his plans lacked foresight and his actions lacked righteousness,
was he not of the same ilk as Chǔ's Bái Gōng Shèng!
Bái Gōng Shèng wished to avenge his father's enemy,
unable to control his anger,
brought harm upon his uncle,
the event is recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn.
Jīng Kē, harboring personal gratitude for being patronized,
disregarded the seven clans,
Hàn's Zōu Yáng said: Jīng Kē caused the seven clans to be submerged.
Yīng Shào said: Jīng Kē, for attempting to assassinate the King of Qín for Yān,
caused his clan to be implicated and submerged.
Was that not foolish indeed!
Therefore, Yáng Zǐ discussed this,
considering Yào Lí as the mǐ of the spider,
Niè Zhèng as the mǐ of the brave warrior,
Yào Lí,
a man of Wú,
assassinated Qìng Jì for King Hé Lǘ of Wú.
This means his strength was insufficient,
like a spider whose poison stings a person and then perishes.
Mǐ,
means to be routed and perish.
Ěryǎ commentary: zhī [AS-FBEC] miǎn zhū,
is zhū máo.
Fāngyán: West of the pass,
in the regions of Qín and Jìn, it is called zhū máo,
in the regions of Zhào and Wèi, it is called zhī [AS-FBEC] miǎn zhū.
Zhū,
is pronounced zhū;
máo,
is pronounced máo.
Mǐ,
in Wēn Gōng's commentary on Yáng Zǐ,
is pronounced according to its usual reading.
Kāng gives měi wéi qiē,
meaning to be crushed to pieces.
I say Kāng's pronunciation and meaning are both incorrect.
Niè Zhèng's affair is recorded in the fifth year of King Ān in the first scroll.
None can be called righteous.
He also said:
"Jīng Kē,
a gentleman would call him a robber."
Wú Mì said: Jīng Kē,
if judged by the standards of a gentleman, is but a robber.
2 Wáng Bēn attacked Dài,
and captured the King of Dài, Jiā.
Jiā fled to Dài,
see the nineteenth year in the previous scroll, when Zhào ceased its sacrifices.
3 Wáng Jiǎn completely pacified the lands of Jīng and south of the Jiāng,
subjugating the lords of the Bǎi Yuè,
and established Kuàijī Commandery.
Qín's Kuàijī Commandery was administered from Wú County,
encompassing the present-day Mǐnyuè and the lands of Liǎng Zhè.
Later Hàn divided Kuàijī to establish Wú Commandery,

Liú Shù said: Yǔ convened the feudal lords south of the Jiāng and achieved merit,
therefore named the mountain Kuàijī,

Kuài,
is pronounced gǔ wài fān.
4 In the fifth month,
a great celebration was held throughout the land.
5. Initially,
the Queen Dowager of Qí was virtuous.
(The Queen Dowager,
daughter of Tàishǐ Jiǎo,
was Queen to King Xiāng.)
She kept faith with the other feudal lords;
moreover, Qí's eastern border was on the sea.
(This means Qí extended eastward to take the island barbarians,
using the sea as its border.)
Another view states: Because Qí's eastern border was on the sea,
it did not share a border with Qín,
and therefore did not suffer military attacks.
The other five states each sought their own salvation,
and for this reason, King Jiàn of Qí reigned for over forty years without suffering military attack.
When the Queen Dowager was about to die,
she cautioned King Jiàn, saying:
"Among the ministers, So-and-so is worthy of employment."
The King said:
"Please write it down."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Very well!"
The King took brush and tablet to receive her words,
but the Queen Dowager then said:
"This old woman has already forgotten."
After the Queen Dowager died,
Hòu Shèng became Chancellor of Qí.
(The Surname Genealogy states: The surname Hòu originally was Hòu,
and later they removed
the '邑' radical.)
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: Shèng
is pronounced shēng.
When guests and retainers went to Qín,
Qín also gave them much gold.
These guests all acted as spies,
urging the King to pay court to Qín,
not to cultivate preparations for attack and defense,
and not to aid the five states in attacking Qín.
Qín, for this reason, was able to destroy the five states.
When the King of Qí was about to go to pay court [to Qín],
the Commandant of the Yōng Gate stepped forward and said:
(Zuǒzhuàn: When Jìn besieged Qí,
they cut down the catalpas at the Yōng Gate.
Dù Yù said: Yōng Gate
was a gate of the Qí city wall.
Jīngdiǎn Shìwén: Yōng
is pronounced yòng;
Kāng [Yīn] gives yú lóng qiē,
which is incorrect.)
"For what purpose was a king established?
Was it for the altars of soil and grain,
or for the king himself?"
The King said:
"For the altars of soil and grain."
The Commandant said:
"If a king is established for the altars of soil and grain,
then why does the king abandon the altars of soil and grain to go to Qín?"
(Mèngzǐ said: The people are of supreme importance; the altars of soil and grain come next; the sovereign is of lesser importance.)
The Grand Master of Jímò heard of this
and went to see the King of Qí, saying:
"The territory of Qí extends several
thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several million.
All the Grand Masters of the Three Jìn are ill-disposed towards Qín,
and there are over a hundred of them in the area between Ā and Zhēn;
if Your Majesty gathers them and gives them a host of a million men,
ordering them to recover the former territories of the Three Jìn,
then the pass of Línjìn can be entered.
(Gathering the troops of the Three Jìn and attacking Qín from Hédōng would then allow entry through the Línjìn Pass.)
And there are over a hundred [of such men] south of the city wall;
('south of the city wall'
means below Nánchéng.
Nánchéng
is what King Wēi of Qí ordered Tánzǐ to guard.)
If you order them to recover the former territories of Chǔ,
then the Wǔ Pass can be entered.
(Chǔ attacks Qín from Nányáng to enter the Wǔ Pass.)
Then the majesty of Qí can be established,
and the state of Qín can be destroyed.
How could this be merely preserving one's own state!"
The King of Qí would not listen.
1. Wáng Bēn attacked Qí from the south of Yān,
suddenly entering Línzī.
None of the people dared to resist.
(Gé,
pronounced according to its usual reading,
means to stop,
to fight.)
[Qín] promised to enfeoff [the King of Qí] with a territory of five hundred lǐ.
The King of Qí then surrendered.
Qín moved him to Gòng.
(Bǎn Zhì states:
the Hénèi Commandery had Gòng County.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: Now Wèi Prefecture has Gòngchéng County.)
(Gòng,
pronounced gōng;
the same below.)
He starved to death.
The people of Qí resented King Jiàn for not early allying with the other feudal lords in a vertical alliance,
and for listening to treacherous men and guests, thereby losing his state.
They sang of it, saying:
"O pine,
O cypress!
Was it guests who made Jiàn dwell in Gòng?"
They hated that Jiàn's employment of guests was inauspicious.
(Suǒyǐn states: This means he did not carefully examine and employ his guests,
not knowing whether they were good or bad.)
Thus the Tián clan of Qí perished.
Your servant Guāng remarks: Although the theories of the Vertical and Horizontal alliances were repeatedly argued back and forth,
their main point was that the Vertical alliance
was beneficial to the six states.
In ancient times, the former kings established ten thousand states
and treated the feudal lords with kinship,
having them attend court and present gifts to interact with each other,
hold feasts and banquets to delight each other,
and convene meetings and alliances to bind themselves together.
There was no other reason
than the desire for them to be of one heart and join forces to protect their families and states.
If the six states had been able to treat each other with trust and righteousness,
then even though Qín was strong and violent,
how could it have destroyed them?
Now, the Three Jìn were
the protective screen for Qí and Chǔ;
Qí and Chǔ were
the root and foundation for the Three Jìn.
Their strategic positions supported each other;
exterior and interior depended on one another.
Therefore, for the Three Jìn to attack Qí and Chǔ
was to sever their own root and foundation;
for Qí and Chǔ to attack the Three Jìn
was to remove their own protective screen.
How could there be removing one's own protective screen to curry favor with a robber,
saying,
"The robber will love me and not attack,"
is this not perverse!
2. When the King first unified all under heaven,
he considered himself to possess the virtue that combined that of the Three Sovereigns,
and achievements surpassing those of the Five Emperors.
(Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Huángdì are the Three Sovereigns.
Shàohào, Zhuānxū, Gāoxīn, Táng Yáo, and Yú Shùn are the Five Emperors.
Sòng Jūn’s commentary on the Yuánshénqì quotes Zhēn Yàodù as saying: Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Suìrén are the Three Sovereigns.
Huángdì, Zhuānxū, Dì Kù, Táng Yáo, and Yú Shùn are the Five Emperors.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the Chìshěngtú quotes the Yùndǒushū: Fúxī, Nǚwā, and Shénnóng are the Three Sovereigns.
As for the Five Emperors,
those whose virtue matched the stars of the Five Emperor Seats were called Emperors;
these are Huángdì, Jīntiānshì, Gāoyángshì, Gāoxīnshì, Táotángshì, and Yǒuyúshì.
In reality there are six but they are called five,
because they all matched the stars of the Five Emperor Seats.
The Báihǔtōng takes Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Zhùróng as the Three Sovereigns.
The term “Emperor” (Dì)
is one name for Heaven,
hence it is used to name the ruler.
“Emperor” (Dì)
means “to examine thoroughly” (dì),
signifying that Heaven is vast and without partiality,
forgetting distinctions between self and others,
fair, impartial, and far-reaching,
handling affairs with careful scrutiny,
thus it is called “Emperor.”
The title “Emperor” is equivalent to Heaven,
no name surpasses it,
yet the term “Sovereign” (Huáng) is added,
because “Sovereign” is a name denoting greatness and excellence,
meaning greater than “Emperor.”)
“The Emperor’s”
commands are to be called
“Decrees” (zhì),
and his orders are to be called
“Edicts” (zhào).
(Yán Shígǔ said: The words of the Son of Heaven,
one type is called “Decree documents,”
the second type is called “Edict documents.”
“Decree documents”
refer to commands establishing institutions.
Rú Chún said: “Edict” (zhào)
means “to announce.”
Before the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
only the Son of Heaven could use this term.)
(Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.)
“Zhèn.”
In ancient times, both rulers and ministers commonly used the term “zhèn”;
but since the Qín established the rule,
only the Son of Heaven exclusively uses it.)
“Tàishàng”
is a title of utmost honor.
Since Shǐ Huángdì styled himself “First Emperor,”
he posthumously honored King Zhuāngxiāng as “Tàishàng Huáng.”
From Hàn Gāodì using it to honor his father Tàigōng,
thereafter it was no longer used as a posthumous title.)
“If after death one’s conduct is used to determine a posthumous title (shì),
then it means sons criticizing their father,
ministers criticizing their ruler;
this is utterly meaningless.
From now on,
abolish the system of posthumous titles.
(The Duke of Zhōu created the system of posthumous titles,
establishing titles based on the goodness or evil of one’s conduct.
For rulers like Yōu and Lì,
even if they had filial sons and devoted grandsons,
for a hundred generations they could not change it.
Now Qín abolishes it,
fearing that later generations would give them evil posthumous titles.)
(Shì,
pronounced shén zhì fān.)
Let later generations count by generations,
second generation, third generation, up to ten thousand generations,
passing it on endlessly.”)
3. Earlier,
during the times of Qí Wēiwáng and Xuānwáng,
Zōu Yǎn wrote on the cyclical succession of the Five Virtues;
(the so-called cyclical succession of the Five Virtues means: Fúxī ruled by the virtue of Wood;
Wood generates Fire,
therefore Shénnóng ruled by the virtue of Fire;
Fire generates Earth,
therefore Huángdì ruled by the virtue of Earth;
Earth generates Metal,
therefore Shàohào ruled by the virtue of Metal;
Metal generates Water,
therefore Zhuānxū ruled by the virtue of Water;
Water generates Wood,
therefore Dì Kù again ruled by the virtue of Wood;
Wood again generates Fire,
therefore Dì Yáo ruled by the virtue of Fire;
Fire again generates Earth,
therefore Dì Shùn ruled by the virtue of Earth;
Earth again generates Metal,
therefore the Xià ruled by the virtue of Metal;
Metal again generates Water,
therefore the Shāng ruled by the virtue of Water;
Water again generates Wood,
therefore the Zhōu ruled by the virtue of Wood: this is the cycle of the Five Virtues ending and beginning anew.
Zōu Yǎn believed that Zhōu obtained the virtue of Fire,
probably because the “fire flowing over the royal house” was an omen of Zhōu receiving the Mandate,
and also because its ceremonial color revered red.
Following Yǎn’s theory of cycles,
Qín should take Earth as its element.
Now Shǐ Huángdì, with Water conquering Fire,
himself took Water as his element,
which is the so-called “pushing the Five Conquests.”
At the beginning of Hàn, they took Earth as their element,
probably also following Yǎn’s theory.)
People from Qí presented this [to the court].
Shǐ Huángdì adopted their theory,
believing that Zhōu obtained the virtue of Fire,
and Qín succeeded Zhōu,
following what it could not conquer,
thus taking Water as its virtue.
He began to change the calendar year,
with court congratulations all starting on the first day of the tenth month;
clothing, banners, and flags all revered black;
and the number six was taken as the standard.
(The phrase “changed the calendar year” should be punctuated here.
Xià took the month of Jiànyín as the start of the year,
Yīn took the month of Jiànchǒu as the start of the year,
Zhōu took the month of Jiànzǐ as the start of the year;

“King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed many sons, younger brothers, and relatives of the same surname,

attacking each other like enemies,

Luóchuān County was renamed Zhēnníng County.
Bān's Table of Officials: Commandant Protector of the Army,
a Qín office.
Also,
the King of Hàn appointed Chén Píng as Commandant of the Center Protecting the Army,
overseeing all generals.
At that time,
Tián had already been handed over to the officials,
and fearing mutiny in his army,
they appointed a retainer of Lǐ Sī as Commandant Protector of the Army,
to oversee the generals.
When Hú Hài heard of Fú Sū's death,
he intended to release Méng Tián.
Meanwhile, Méng Yì had gone out to pray to the mountains and rivers for the First Emperor,
and was returning.
Zhào Gāo said to Hú Hài:
"The late Emperor long wished to promote a worthy and establish a Crown Prince,
but Yì advised against it, considering it improper;
it would be better to execute him!"
So he was imprisoned in Dài.
According to geography,
Dài is very far from Shāqiū.
It seems Yì returned to Dài,
and was imprisoned there.
They then proceeded from Jǐngxíng to Jiǔyuán.
Bān's Treatise: Jǐngxíng is west of Shíyì County in Chángshān.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The old Jǐngxíng Pass is eighteen lǐ east of Shí'ài County in Bìngzhōu,
which is the Jǐngxíng Pass.
The hearse carriage became foul-smelling,
so they ordered the accompanying officials to load a shí of salted fish onto a cart to mask the odor.
Mèng Kāng said: One hundred twenty catties is called a shí.
Bān's Treatise on Trade and Biographies: A thousand jūn of zhé and bào fish.
Master Yán's commentary states: Zhé
is dried fish,
which is today's unsalted dried fish.
Bào,
is today's yè fish.
Yet some commentators read bào as wéi fish's wéi,
which is far from the correct meaning.
Zhèng Kāngchéng said yè fish is dried in a bì chamber,
which is also incorrect.
Drying in a bì chamber
produces bào.
It is what people in Bā and Jīng call jiǎn fish today.
The Qín Emperor loaded bào fish to confuse the foul smell,
meaning it was yè fish;
whereas fish dried in a bì chamber
originally is not foul-smelling.
Bào
is pronounced bái mǎo fān.
Zhé
is pronounced jiē.
Yè
is pronounced yú yè fān.
Wéi
is pronounced wǔ huí fān.
Bì
is pronounced pú běi fān.
Jiǎn
is pronounced jū yǎn fān.
They announced the funeral.
The Straight Road,
is the one Méng Tián constructed in the thirty-fifth year.
In the ninth month,
the First Emperor was buried at Líshān.
The tomb was sealed down to the triple springs.
Master Gǔ commented: "Triple springs means three layers of springs,
indicating it reached the water."
I believe 'sealing' refers to
smelting copper to seal and block it.
'Triple springs'
refers to the number nine springs.
Relocated treasures filled it.
This means moving items from the treasury to fill the tomb's side chambers.
'Cáng' (藏)
is pronounced cáng, with the tone cái làng fān.
Anyone who dug near it was shot.
Mercury was used to create the hundred rivers, the great rivers, and the vast seas,
with mechanisms to circulate it.
Kāng's commentary quotes Liú Bózhuāng: "Mechanisms to circulate it
were to prevent those who might dig near."
I consider the literary flow:
from the crossbow traps to 'was shot,'
the meaning is already complete;
'mechanisms to circulate it'
follows the idea of using mercury for the rivers and seas.
Viewed this way,
the text flows smoothly.
'Shè' (射)
is pronounced shè, with the tone ér yì fān.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: 'Guàn' (灌)
is pronounced guǎn.
'Shū' (輸)
is pronounced shù.
The geographical details are below.
Palace women who had no children
were all ordered to follow in death.
After the burial was completed,
someone said the craftsmen who built the mechanical traps
all knew about them,
and if the treasures were heavy, secrets would leak.
Once the great affairs were finished,
they were shut inside the tomb.
'If the treasures were heavy, secrets would leak'
means if the craftsmen built a second layer of mechanical traps,
being close to outsiders,
they would reveal the secrets of the mechanisms.
Therefore, once the great affairs were finished, they were all shut in the tomb.
'Once the great affairs were finished'
is the end of the sentence,
meaning after the interment,
the great affairs of sending off the deceased were complete.
'Zhòng' (重)
is pronounced zhòng, with the tone zhí lóng fān.
2. The Second Emperor wanted to execute Méng Tián and his brothers.
The Second Emperor's nephew Zǐyīng remonstrated:
"King Qiān of Zhào killed Lǐ Mù and employed Yán Jù,
King Jiàn of Qí killed his longtime loyal ministers and employed Hòu Shèng,
and in the end, both states perished.
Both events were seen earlier.
'Zú' (卒)
is pronounced zú, with the tone zǐ xù fān.
They are great ministers and strategists of Qín,
yet Your Majesty wishes to discard them in a single day.
To kill loyal ministers and establish those without integrity
is to cause distrust among ministers internally and alienate the fighting men externally!"
The Second Emperor did not listen
and proceeded to kill Méng Yì and the Neishi Méng Tián.
Méng Tián said:
"From my ancestors to my descendants,
we have accumulated merit and trust in Qín for three generations.
Méng Tián's grandfather Ào, father Wǔ, and Méng Tián himself
all served Qín with merit for three generations.
Though I am imprisoned,
my influence is enough to rebel.
Yet I know I must die and uphold righteousness,
not daring to disgrace my ancestors' teachings and not forgetting the First Emperor!"
He then took poison and killed himself.
The Yángzǐ Fǎyán says: Someone asked:
"Méng Tián was loyal yet executed;
is loyalty worthwhile?"
The reply:
"Cutting through mountains,
filling valleys,
starting from Líntáo,
reaching Liáoshuǐ,
strength insufficient yet corpses abundant—
his loyalty was not enough to assist."
Your subject Guāng says: The First Emperor was poisoning the world, and Méng Tián acted as his agent;
Méng Tián's lack of benevolence is evident.
However,
Méng Tián understood the duty of a minister.
Though executed without crime,
he could hold fast to death without disloyalty,
which is also worthy of praise.
'Shǐ' (使)
is pronounced as the character.
The First Emperor of the Second Generation
was named Húhài,
the youngest son of the First Emperor.
[Chapter note: The twelve-line edition lacks these eight characters;
the eleven-line edition is the same.]
1. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Wùyín day,
a great amnesty was declared.
2. In spring,
the Second Emperor traveled east through the commanderies and counties,
with Lǐ Sī accompanying;
they reached Jiéshí,
followed the coast,
and went south to Kuàijī;
and inscribed on all the steles erected by the First Emperor,
adding the names of the accompanying ministers,
to glorify the former emperor's achievements and abundant virtue before returning.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the Second Emperor returned to Xiányáng
and said to Zhào Gāo:
"A person's life in this world
is like six steeds galloping past a crack.
Since I rule the world,
I wish to indulge all my sensory pleasures,
exhaust all delights of heart and mind,
to spend my remaining years.
Is this possible?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"This is what a worthy ruler can do, but a foolish and chaotic ruler forbids.
However,
there are concerns that cannot be ignored.
Allow me to explain: The Shāqiū plot,
the various princes and ministers all doubted it;
and the princes are all Your Majesty's elder brothers,
and the ministers were appointed by the former emperor.
Now that Your Majesty has just ascended,
these people are discontent and不服,
fearing they may rebel;
I tremble with fear,
only worried it will not end well.
How can Your Majesty indulge in such pleasures!"
The Second Emperor said:
"What should be done?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Your Majesty should enforce strict laws and harsh punishments,
decree mutual implication for crimes,
execute ministers and the imperial clan;
then gather and promote the remaining people,
enriching the poor,
ennobling the lowly.
Completely remove the former emperor's old ministers,
and replace them with those Your Majesty trusts.
Then hidden virtue will return to Your Majesty,
harm eliminated and treacherous plots blocked,
all ministers will receive favor,
and enjoy great kindness.
Your Majesty can then rest easy and indulge in pleasure.
No plan is better than this!"
The Second Emperor agreed.
He then revised the laws,
making them even harsher.
When ministers or princes committed crimes,
they were handed to Zhào Gāo
for interrogation.
Thus, twelve princes were executed in the Xiányáng market,
ten princesses were killed at Dù,
their property confiscated by the state treasury.
Hàn referred to the Son of Heaven as the state treasury.
This 'state treasury'
means the public treasury.
Those implicated were all arrested.
Gòngfù said: If the person is alive,
directly pursuing and capturing is called 'dài' (逮);
if the person is dead,
then apprehending and seizing is called 'bǔ' (捕).
'Dài' (逮)
is an easier term;
'bǔ' (捕)
involves more force.
The brothers of Prince Jiānglǘ, three in total, were imprisoned in the inner palace,
and their crimes were deliberated upon last.
The Second Emperor sent an envoy to command Jiānglǘ, saying:
"You, Prince, have failed in your duties as a subject,
a crime punishable by death!"
The officials then carried out the sentence.
Jiānglǘ said:
"In the rituals of the court,
I have never dared to disobey the protocol of the guests and officials;
in the positions of the temple and court,
I have never dared to neglect proper conduct;
in receiving orders and responding,
I have never dared to utter improper words;
how can this be called failing in my duties as a subject?
I dare not rely on the affection of kinship to abandon the duties of a subject,
how can such a crime be imposed upon me!"
The envoy said:
"I, as a subject, cannot participate in the deliberation,
I merely carry out the orders as written!"
Jiānglǘ then raised his head to the sky and cried out
"Heaven"
three times,
saying:
"I am innocent!"
The three brothers all shed tears,
drew their swords, and committed suicide.
The imperial clan trembled in fear.
Prince Gāo wished to flee,
but feared that his entire clan would be arrested,
so he submitted a memorial, saying:
"When the late emperor was in good health,
I, as a subject, upon entering the palace,
was granted food,
and when leaving, rode in the imperial carriage;
the garments from the imperial wardrobe,
I was granted them;
the treasured horses from the stables,
I was granted them.
I should have followed in death but could not,
as a son, I am unfilial,
as a subject, I am disloyal.
One who is unfilial and disloyal
has no name to stand in this world.
I request to follow in death,
and wish to be buried at the foot of Líshān.
May Your Majesty have pity and grant this wish!"
The memorial was submitted,
and the Second Emperor was greatly pleased.
He summoned Zhào Gāo and showed it to him,
saying:
"Can this be considered urgent?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Subjects should be too preoccupied with worrying about death,
how could they have time to plot rebellion!"
The Second Emperor approved his memorial,
granting one hundred thousand coins for his burial.
The construction of the Ēpáng Palace resumed.
Fifty thousand skilled men were conscripted to garrison Xiányáng,
and were ordered to practice archery.
As there were many dogs, horses, and other animals to feed,
and supplies were insufficient,
orders were issued to the commanderies and counties,
to transport beans, grains, fodder, and straw,
all required to bring their own rations;
within three hundred lǐ of Xiányáng, no one was allowed to consume its grain.
3 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Chén Shèng from Yángchéng and Wú Guǎng from Yángjiǎ raised troops in Qí.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: This refers to Yángchéng County in Hénán;
according to Bān Zhì,
it belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Yángjiǎ County belonged to the Kingdom of Huáiyáng.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Tàikāng County in Chén Prefecture,
was originally the territory of Hàn's Yángjiǎ County.
Pánzhōu Hóng shì states: Yángjiǎ Township is thirty lǐ from Tàikāng County.
Jiǎ,
is pronounced as jiǎ.
According to Bān Zhì,
Qí County belonged to Pèi Commandery,
and contained Dàzé Township.
Qí,
is pronounced as qú yī fān.
They conscripted the men from the left side of the village gates to garrison Yúyáng.
Cháo Cuò said: Qín used convicts for garrison duty,
first conscripting officials who had committed offenses, as well as sons-in-law living with their wives' families and merchants,
then those who had once been registered as merchants,
then those whose grandparents had once been registered as merchants,
and finally entering the village gates to take those from the left side.
Suǒyǐn states: Lǘzuǒ,
refers to those living on the left side of the village.
During the Qín era,
those exempted from corvée lived on the left side.
Now, all those on the left side were conscripted for labor service.
It also states: Generally, the wealthy and powerful lived on the right,
while the poor and weak lived on the left.
Qín's garrison duties mostly involved the wealthy;
when these were exhausted,
they also conscripted the poor and weak.
According to Bān Zhì,
Yúyáng County belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Yúyáng is eighteen lǐ south of Mìyún County in Tán Prefecture,
located north of the Yú River.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng were both appointed as troop leaders.
Shī Gǔ states: A group of people gathered together is called a tún.
A leader,
is a commander.
It happened that heavy rain fell,
making the roads impassable,
and they estimated they would miss the deadline;
missing the deadline,
according to the law, meant execution for all.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng, capitalizing on the widespread resentment and grievances of the people,
killed the commanding captain.
Shī Gǔ states: This officer was originally just a captain,
but because he was leading the garrison troops at the time,
he was called the commanding captain.
Suǒyǐn states: Wèi,
is an official title;
according to the Hàn Jiùyí: Large counties had three such officials.
This captain was leading a garrison of nine hundred men,
hence he was called the commanding captain.
"All of you have missed the deadline and face execution;
even if you are not executed,
six or seven out of ten of those sent to garrison duty will die anyway.
Moreover, if a brave man does not die, that is all;
if he must die, he should die for a great cause!
Are kings, marquises, generals, and ministers born to their stations?!"
The crowd all followed them.
They then falsely claimed to be acting under the authority of Prince Fú Sū and Xiàng Yān,
because the common people admired Fú Sū and the people of Chǔ sympathized with Xiàng Yān.
They proclaimed the name "Great Chǔ";
Chén Shèng appointed himself as general,
and Wú Guǎng as commandant.
They attacked Dàzé Township,
and captured it;
gathering their forces, they attacked Qí,
and Qí fell.
They gathered the troops from Dàzé Township to attack Qí.
They attacked Zhì, Cuó, Kǔ, Zhè, and Qiáo,
and captured them all.
Bān Zhì states: Fúlí, Zhì, Cuó, and Qiáo belonged to Pèi Commandery.
The Xìngpǔ states: After the state of Gé was destroyed,
its descendants took the state name as their surname.
Zhè
and Kǔ counties belonged to the Kingdom of Huáiyáng.
Sòng Bái states: Zhè County,
was the ancient settlement of the Xiāng clan;
during the Spring and Autumn period,
it was Zhūyě of Chén;
in Hàn times it was Zhè County,
named after the Zhè Ditch within its borders;
in Táng times it was Zhèchéng County in Sòng Prefecture.
Zhēnyuán County in Bó Prefecture,
was the ancient territory of Kǔ County.
Xùn,
is pronounced cí jùn fān,
meaning to overrun territory.
Zhì,
is pronounced zhú yǐ fān.
"Cuó",
originally written as
is pronounced cái duō fān.
Shī Gǔ states: This county originally borrowed the character "酇" for its name,
pronounced cuó.
Wáng Mǎng changed the county's name to Zànzhì,
so this county also has the pronunciation zàn.
Kǔ,
is pronounced hù.
By the time they reached Chén,
they had six to seven hundred chariots,
over a thousand cavalry,
and tens of thousands of infantry.
They attacked Chén.
The governor and commandant of Chén were both absent,
only the acting assistant resisted and fought with them at the watchtower gate,
but was defeated;
the acting assistant died,
and Chén Shèng then entered and occupied Chén.
According to Bān Zhì,
Chén County belonged to the Kingdom of Huáiyáng.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: The present-day city of Chén Prefecture was originally the city of the state of Chén built by King Xiāng of Chǔ.
Shī Gǔ states: Shǒuchéng refers to the commandery assistant who remained in charge of the defense;
one interpretation: it is the assistant to the commandery governor,
hence called shǒuchéng.
Yuánfù states: Qín did not make Chén a commandery,
so how could it have a governor?
Shǒu here means not the regular official,
but someone temporarily acting in charge.
I note that Qín divided the empire into commanderies and counties,
commanderies had governors, commandants, and inspectors,
counties had magistrates, assistants, and captains.
Yuánfù's interpretation of this shǒu as a temporary acting position
is quite correct.
The histories by Simǎ Qiān and Bān Gù write
"the governor and magistrate were both absent",
while here it is written
"the governor and commandant were both absent".
Probably in the two histories,
the character "magistrate"
is missing the following
"commandant"
character,
and in the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,
the character "commandant"
is missing the preceding
"magistrate"
character.
Shī Gǔ states: Qiáomén refers to a gate with a tall tower built above it for observation.
Such a tower,
is also called a qiáo,
hence a beautiful tower is called a lìqiáo;
it is also called a cháo.
The so-called cháochē [nest cart]
also had a tower built on a war chariot to observe the enemy.
Qiáo and cháo
have similar pronunciations.
Initially,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú of Dàliáng formed a friendship sworn to the death.
When Qín destroyed Wèi,
hearing that these two were renowned scholars of Wèi,
they offered heavy rewards to capture them.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú then changed their names and surnames,
and together went to Chén.
They served as village gatekeepers to support themselves.
Master Yán Gǔ said: Gatekeepers,
are the lowliest of soldiers;
Ěr and Yú hid themselves in humble positions.
Zhāng Yàn said: Gatekeepers,
are guards of the village head.
Jiān,
is pronounced as "jiān" in ancient times.
Chén Yú wanted to rise up,
but Zhāng Ěr stepped on his foot,
making him endure the flogging.
"Wanted to rise up" means
he could not bear the humiliation,
and wished to rise and confront the official.
Niè,
is pronounced as "niè,"
meaning to step on his foot.
Chī,
is pronounced as "chī."
Zhāng Ěr then led Chén Yú under a mulberry tree,
and admonished him, saying:
"What did I tell you from the beginning?
Now, over a minor insult, you would risk your life against an official!"
Chén Yú apologized to him.
After Chén Shè entered Chén,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú went to his gate to pay their respects.
Chén Shèng,
styled Shè.
He was greatly pleased.
The local elders and heroes of Chén requested that Shè be made King of Chǔ,
and Shè consulted Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú about it.
Ěr and Yú replied:
"Qín is without virtue,
destroying the altars of states,
and oppressing the people;
you, General, have risked your life
to rid the world of this scourge.
Now, upon first arriving in Chén, you proclaim yourself king,
showing the world your selfishness.
We hope you will not become king,
but instead quickly lead your troops westward;
send men to reestablish the descendants of the Six States,
thereby building alliances for yourself,
and increasing the enemies of Qín;
with more enemies, their strength will be divided,
and with allies, your military will be strong.
In this way,
there will be no battles in the countryside,
and all Six States will become your allies,
so no troops will clash in the fields.
All counties will rebel against Qín and restore the great states,
and none will remain to guard cities for Qín.
Seize Xiányáng,
and command the feudal lords;
the feudal lords, having been destroyed and then restored,
will submit to your virtue,
and then
your imperial enterprise will be achieved!
Now, if you alone make Chén your kingdom,
I fear the world will grow lax."
Chén Shè did not listen,
and instead proclaimed himself king,
with the title
"Zhāng Chǔ."
Liú Dé said: It is as if to say, "Expand the great state of Chǔ."
Zhāng Yàn said: Previously, Chǔ had already been destroyed by Qín,
and now Chǔ is established to expand it.
At that time,
the commanderies and counties suffered under Qín's laws,
and they vied to kill their chief officials in response to Shè.
A court usher
came from the east,
and reported the rebellion.
Èrshì was enraged,
and handed him over to the officials.
When later envoys arrived,
the emperor questioned them,
and they replied:
"They are but petty thieves, pilfering like mice and dogs;
the commandery governors and commandants are pursuing and capturing them,
and they will soon all be caught,
not worth worrying about."
The emperor was pleased.
King Chén appointed Wú Shū as acting king,
to oversee the generals in attacking Xíngyáng to the west.
Wú Guǎng,
styled Shū.
Xíngyáng County belonged to Sānchuān Commandery.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú again advised King Chén,
requesting a surprise force to campaign northward and seize Zhào territory.
Thereupon, King Chén appointed Wǔ Chén, a man of Chén whom he had previously befriended, as general,
and Shào Sāo as army supervisor.
The surname genealogy says: The surname Wǔ
descends from Duke Wǔ of Sòng.
I say: Since the establishment of posthumous titles,
many have taken "Wǔ" as their posthumous title;
yet to insist that the surname Wǔ must descend from Duke Wǔ of Sòng,
how rigid is that!
The Táng Dynasty clan records consider the Wǔ clan to descend from the Jī surname,
as the youngest son of King Píng of Zhōu was born with the character
"Wǔ" on his hand,
and thus took it as his surname.
This explanation arose due to Empress Wǔ and was fabricated accordingly.
Zhào Míngchéng's "Jīnshí Lù" includes the stele of Wǔ Bān, the Chief Clerk of Dūnhuáng in the Hàn Dynasty, which states: In ancient times, King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn conquered the Guǐfāng,
and his official clan divided,
thus taking it as their surname.
The surname Shào,
descends from Shào Gōng Shì, son of King Wén of Zhōu;
some say it descends from the eleventh son, Dān Jì Zǎi.
He was given three thousand soldiers,
to subdue Zhào.
King Chén also ordered Dèng Zōng of Rǔyīn to subdue Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
King Wǔ Dīng of Yīn enfeoffed his uncle north of the Yellow River,
making him Marquis of Dèng,
and later generations took this as their surname.
According to Bān's records,
Rǔyīn County belonged to Rǔnán Commandery,
formerly the state of Hú.
Jiǔjiāng,
originally Chǔ territory,
after Qín destroyed Chǔ,
it was divided to establish Jiǔjiāng Commandery;
after Xiàng Yǔ destroyed Qín,
he enfeoffed it to Qíng Bù;
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn renamed it the Huáinán Kingdom;
Emperor Wǔ restored it as Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
Chǔ troops, numbering in the thousands and gathering in groups, were countless.
Gé Yīng reached Dōngchéng,
according to Bān's records,
Dōngchéng County belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
"Kuòdìzhì": The old city of Dōngchéng
is fifty lǐ southeast of Dìngyuǎn County in Háo Prefecture.
The surname genealogy: Xiāng,
descends from Xiāng Zhòng, son of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ.
He then killed Xiāng Qiáng and returned to report.
King Chén executed Gé Yīng.
King Chén ordered
Zhōu Fú to campaign northward and subdue Wèi territory.
He appointed Cài Cì of Shàngcài, the Lord of Fáng, as Supreme Pillar of State.
Suǒ Yǐn said: Fáng,
is the name of a fief;
he was enfeoffed at Fáng,
and titled Lord of Fáng.
Supreme Pillar of State,
is the highest noble title of Chǔ.
Cài,
took the state as their surname.
King Chén heard of Zhōu Wén,
a worthy man of Chén;
skilled in military affairs,
he thus gave him a general's seal,
and sent him west to attack Qín.
Wǔ Chén and others crossed the river from Báimǎ.
Shī Gǔ notes: Báimǎ Ford is located within the boundaries of present-day Báimǎ County in Huá Prefecture.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Báimǎ
is twenty-four lǐ southwest of Wèinán County in Huá Prefecture.
Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēngjì says: The old city of Báimǎ was the Cáo settlement of Wèi.
They persuaded the local heroes and leaders,
and the heroes and leaders all responded to them;
then they marched to gather troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men;
they hailed Wǔ Chén as Lord Wǔxìn.
They captured over ten cities in Zhào,
while the rest all defended their cities;
so they led their troops northeast to attack Fànyáng.
Bān Zhì states,
Fànyáng County belonged to Zhuō Commandery.
Yìng Shào says: It was located on the north bank of the Fàn River.
Kuǎi Chè,
also known as Kuǎi Tōng,
Bān's history avoids Emperor Wǔ's personal name,
thus changing
"Chè"
to
"Tōng".
Kuǎi,
pronounced qiū guài fān,
is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn records
that in Jìn there was a senior official named Kuǎi Dé.
"If you, sir, insist on fighting and winning before seizing territory,
attacking and capturing before taking cities,
I humbly believe this is a mistake.
If you truly heed my plan,
