and Lǐ Guī and others died.
Yángchéng man Dèng Yuè led troops stationed at Tán,
and a separate general under Zhāng Hán attacked and defeated him.
Zhì man Wǔ Féng led troops stationed at Xǔ.
Wǔ
is a surname.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Chǔ had Wǔ Jǔ and Wǔ Shē.
Xǔ
was the state of the Xǔzǐ in the Spring and Autumn period.
According to Bān's Treatise, it belonged to Yǐngchuān;
Wèi Wéndì changed it to Xǔchāng;
in Táng times, it was Xǔ Prefecture.
Both armies scattered,
fleeing to Chén,
and King Chén executed Dèng Yuè.
3 The Second Emperor repeatedly reprimanded and reproached Lǐ Sī:
"You occupy the position of one of the Three Dukes,
how can you let the bandits become like this!"
Lǐ Sī, fearful and apprehensive,
valuing his noble rank and emolument,
did not know what course to take.
He then pandered to the Second Emperor's wishes,
and in a written response said:
"Now, a worthy ruler
must be one capable of implementing the methods of supervision and accountability.
Sǒu Yǐn says: 'Supervision' means
to investigate;
to investigate their crimes,
and hold them accountable with punishments.
To call it
'using all under heaven as fetters and handcuffs'
means
nothing other than
being unable to supervise and hold accountable,
and instead personally toiling for the people of all under heaven,
like Yáo and Yǔ did;
therefore it is called fetters and handcuffs.'
'Fetters and handcuffs'
are instruments of restraint;
on the feet they are called fetters (zhì),
on the hands they are called handcuffs (gù).
Zhì
is pronounced zhí rì fān.
Gù
is pronounced gū wò fān.
To implement the way of supervision and accountability
is precisely to use all under heaven for one's own comfort;
whereas merely striving to exhaust one's body and weary one's spirit,
sacrificing oneself for the common people,
this is the service of a black-headed subject,
not the nurturing of all under heaven.
How could it be worthy of honor!
Therefore, an enlightened ruler, capable of implementing the methods of supervision and accountability to make decisions alone from above,
ensures that power does not lie with his ministers.
Only then can he obliterate the path of benevolence and righteousness,
cut off the sophistry of remonstrance and persuasion,
and indulge his heart in unrestrained willfulness
with none daring to oppose him.
Like this,
his ministers and the common people will be too busy correcting their own faults,
how would they dare to plot any change!"
The Second Emperor was pleased.
Thereupon, he implemented supervision and accountability even more severely.
Officials who taxed the people heavily were considered enlightened,
those who killed many were considered loyal ministers.
Those being punished filled half the roads,
and the dead formed daily piles in the marketplaces;
the people of Qín grew increasingly terrified and longed for rebellion.
4 Zhào Lǐ Liáng had already pacified Chángshān.
Last year,
King of Zhào had sent Lǐ Liáng to capture Chángshān.
The King of Zhào again sent Liáng to capture Tàiyuán.
Upon reaching Shíyì,
Qín troops blocked Jǐngxíng,
and he could not advance.
Bān Zhì states:
Shíyì County belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
Jǐngxíng Mountain lies to its west.
Block (sāi)
is pronounced xī zé fān.
Xíng
is pronounced xíng.
Liáng, having received a letter (and) not believing it,
returned to Hándān,
to further request troops.
Before arriving,
on the road he encountered the elder sister of the King of Zhào returning from a drinking outing.
Liáng saw her from afar,
thinking it was the king,
and prostrated himself in greeting by the roadside.
The king's sister was drunk,
and did not recognize him as a general.
She sent a rider to dismiss Lǐ Liáng.
Lǐ Liáng had always been esteemed,
he rose,
ashamed before his attending officers.
Having bowed in greeting and risen,
he looked at his attending officers and felt ashamed.
Attending (cóng)
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
"All under heaven has turned against Qín,
the capable rise first.
Moreover, the King of Zhào was originally beneath you, General.
Now this mere woman does not even dismount from her carriage for the General.
I request permission to pursue and kill her!"
Lǐ Liáng had already received the letter from Qín,
and was firmly intending to rebel against Zhào,
but had not yet decided.
Angered by this,
he sent men to pursue and kill the king's sister.
Then, leading his troops, he launched a surprise attack on Hándān.
Hándān was unaware,
and he ultimately killed the King of Zhào and Shào Sāo.
Many among the people of Zhào acted as eyes and ears for Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú,
and for this reason the two alone managed to escape.
'For this reason' means
because of this reason.
5 Qín Jiā of Líng and Zhū Jīshí of Fúlí, among others, raised troops,
besieging the Governor of Dōnghǎi at Tán.
"Chén"
should be
"Líng";
the Biography of Chén Shèng writes
"Qín Jiā of Líng".
Qín
is a surname;
during the Spring and Autumn period,
Lǔ had a Qín Jǐnfù.
Bān Zhì says: Dōnghǎi Commandery,
was established by Emperor Gāo of Hàn;
Yìng Shào's commentary states: It was the Qín Tán Commandery.
According to my examination, the thirty-six commanderies mentioned by Péi Yīn
originally also did not include a Tán Commandery.
The Hàn Dōnghǎi Commandery was simply administered from Tán.
(Chén Shèng) appointed Lord Wǔpíng Pàn as a general,
to oversee the army below Tán.
Qín Jiā did not accept the command,
appointing himself Grand Marshal;
he detested being subordinate to Lord Wǔpíng.
He informed the army officers:
"Lord Wǔpíng is young,
and knows nothing of military affairs.
Do not heed him!"
Thereupon, forging a royal command, he killed Lord Wǔpíng Pàn.
6 The Second Emperor further dispatched Chief Clerk Sīmǎ Xīn and Dǒng Yì to assist Zhāng Hán in attacking the bandits.
At that time, Zhāng Hán was the supreme general,
leading troops east on campaign,
therefore (the Emperor) sent Xīn as Chief Clerk to assist him.
According to the Biography of Xiàng Jí,
Yì was Commandant.
The Surname Register: Liào Shū'ān's descendant Dǒng Fù was fond of dragons,
Emperor Shùn praised him,
and consequently bestowed the surname Dǒng.
(Zhāng Hán) attacked Chén's Pillar of State Lord Fáng,
and killed him;
then advanced to attack Zhāng Hè's army west of Chén.
King Chén supervised the battle.
Zhāng Hè died.
In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Yàn said: The twelfth month of Qín
corresponds to the ninth month of the Xià calendar.
Chén Zàn said: It is the month when the chǒu branch is established.
Yán Shīgǔ said: The Records of the Grand Historian states: In the second year of Húhài, in the tenth month,
Gé Yīng was executed;
in the eleventh month,
Zhōu Wén died;
in the twelfth month,
Chén Shè died: Zàn's explanation is correct.
King Chén went to Rǔyīn,
zhī means
to go to.
He reached Xiàchéngfù.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Xiàchéngfù,
is a place name,
located east of Chéngfù County in Pèi Commandery.
Liú Zhāo said: In Shānsāng County of Rǔnán,
which formerly belonged to Pèi,
there was the settlement of Xiàchéngfù.
Fù
is pronounced fǔ.
Earlier,
after Chén Shè became king,
his old acquaintances all went to rely on him.
His wife's father also went there.
King Chén treated him as one of the many guests,
giving a long bow without kneeling.
His wife's father angrily said:
"You rely on chaos to usurp a title,
and are arrogant towards your elders.
You will not last long!"
He left without saying goodbye.
King Chén knelt and apologized,
but he did not look back.
The guests came and went more freely,
speaking of King Chén's past circumstances.
Someone advised King Chén, saying:
"These guests are foolish and ignorant,
recklessly speaking nonsense,
diminishing your authority."
King Chén executed him.
All the old acquaintances then withdrew on their own,
and from then on, no one was close to King Chén.
King Chén appointed Zhū Fáng as Zhōngzhèng,
Hú Wǔ as Sīguò,
to oversee and control the officials.
When the generals returned from conquering territories,
if their orders were not followed,
they were immediately bound and punished.
They considered harsh scrutiny as loyalty;
those they disliked,
they did not hand over to the officials,
but dealt with them themselves.
The generals, because of this, did not become close or attached to him,
which is why he failed.
The historian states that King Chén abandoned his relatives and old acquaintances,
and thus died at the hands of Zhuāng Gǔ,
so he first uses the term "old acquaintances" to begin the account,
then mentions the disrespect towards his wife's father,
and then the matter of the guests.
The guest had previously plowed as a hired laborer with King Chén.
When King Chén occupied Chén and became king,
the guest blocked the road to request an audience.
King Chén took him in his carriage and returned together;
later, because the guest spoke of his past circumstances,
he killed him.
"Diminishing authority" means
to diminish the dignity and gravity of being a ruler.
Zhuān
is the same as zhuān (to monopolize).
King Chén's former palace attendant general Lǚ Chén formed the Cāngtóu Army.
Wèi had two hundred thousand Cāngtóu troops,
so it seems that the Cāngtóu Army existed before this time.
Yīng Shào said: At that time, the soldiers all wore blue headbands,
hence called Cāngtóu.
Fú Qián said: Cāngtóu
refers to soldiers wearing blue silk headbands,
similar to how the Chìméi were named for identification.
According to Bān's records,
Xīnyáng County belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
Yīng Shào said: It was located north of the Xīn River.
Kuòdìzhì: The old city of Xīnyáng
is forty-two lǐ southwest of Zhēnyáng County in Yùzhōu.
He attacked it,
killed Zhuāng Gǔ,
and again made Chén part of Chǔ;
he buried King Chén in Dàng,
and posthumously honored him as King Yǐn.
Earlier,
King Chén ordered Sòng Liú from Zhì to lead troops to pacify Nányáng,
and enter Wǔguān.
Liú had already conquered Nányáng,
but upon hearing of King Chén's death,
Nányáng returned to Qín control;
Sòng Liú surrendered with his army,
and Èrshì had Liú torn apart by chariots as a warning.
7. Zhōu Fú of Wèi led troops to capture
Fēng and Pèi,
and sent someone to recruit Yōng Chǐ.
Yōng Chǐ had never wanted to submit to the Lord of Pèi,
so he immediately surrendered Fēng to Wèi.
Yǎ
means always.
He did not succeed.
8. Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú of Zhào gathered their scattered troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men,
and attacked Lǐ Liáng;
Liáng was defeated,
and fled back to Zhāng Hán.
A guest advised Ěr and Yú, saying:
"You two gentlemen are travelers,
and wish to attach yourselves to Zhào,
but it is difficult to stand independently;
establish a descendant of Zhào,
assist with righteousness,
and you can achieve merit."
They then sought and found Zhào Xiē.
In spring,
the first month,
Ěr and Yú established Xiē as King of Zhào,
residing in Xìndū.
Xiàng Yǔ changed Xìndū to Xiāngguó;
Hàn restored it as Xìndū County,
belonging to the Xìndū Kingdom;
Later Hàn again called it Xiāngguó.
9. Níng Jūn of Dōngyáng and Qín Jiā
Wén Yǐng said: Qín Jiā was
a man of Dōngyáng Commandery,
and was the lord of Níng County.
Chén Zàn said: In the biography of Chén Shèng,
it says "Qín Jiā of Líng,"
so then Jiā was not from Dōngyáng.
Jiā arose in Tán,
titled Grand Marshal,
and was not the lord of Níng County.
Níng Jūn of Dōngyáng is one person,
and Qín Jiā is another.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Zàn is correct.
Dōngyáng
refers to the county he belonged to;
Níng Jūn means
his surname was Níng,
and he was called Jūn at that time.
According to the genealogy of surnames: He was a descendant of the Níng clan, ministers of Wèi;
also, in Jìn there was Níng Yíng,
who took his fief as his surname.
They then established Jǐng Jū as King of Chǔ,
led troops to Fāngyǔ,
and wanted to attack the Qín army below Dìngtáo;
according to Bān's records,
Fāngyǔ County belonged to Shānyáng Commandery,
and Dìngtáo County belonged to Jìyīn Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Fāngyǔ
is present-day Jìzhōu County;
Dìngtáo
is present-day Cáozhōu County.
Fāngyǔ
is pronounced fáng yù.
They wanted to join forces and advance together.
The King of Qí said:
"King Chén was defeated in battle,
and it is unknown whether he is alive or dead.
How can Chǔ not request permission and establish a king!"
Gōngsūn Qìng said:
"Qí did not request permission from Chǔ to establish a king,
so why should Chǔ request permission from Qí to establish a king!
Moreover, Chǔ took the lead in the affair,
and should give orders to the world."
"Taking the lead in the affair" means
being the first to raise troops against Qín.
The Qín Left and Right Xiào again attacked Chén,
and captured it.
Suǒyǐn says: Left and Right Xiào
refers to the Left and Right Xiàowèi.
Xiào
is pronounced hù jiào.
Scattered troops gathered again.
Rú Chún said: Jiǎo means
to intercept,
meaning scattered troops gathered again.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Jiǎo
is pronounced gōng yáo.
I say that following Rú's explanation,
it should be pronounced yú yáo.
Pó
refers to Póyáng County,
which in Hàn times belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery.
Yīng Bù was a bandit on the river,
and the magistrate of Póyáng, Wú Ruì, gave him his daughter in marriage,
hence he was called the Pó bandit.
Pó
is pronounced pú hé.
They defeated them at Qīngbō,
and again made Chén part of Chǔ.
Qing Bu (Ying Bu) was a native of Lù.
Lù,
in the Spring and Autumn period, was the state of Lù;
under Qin it became a county,
belonging to Jiǔjiāng Commandery;
under Han it belonged to the Kingdom of Liù'ān.
The *Kuòdìzhì* states: The old city of Lù
is located 130 *lǐ* south of Ānfēng County in Shòu Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Present-day Guǎngjì County east of Qí Prefecture is the Lù County of Qin and Han times.
Yīng Bu made Lù his capital,
and the old city walls still remain.
The *Xìngpǔ* states: The Yīng surname originated from the Yǎn surname;
descendants of Gāo Yáo were enfeoffed at Yīng,
and subsequently took this as their clan name.
He was sentenced as a convict and sent to Líshān.
The convicts at Líshān numbered several hundred thousand men.
Bu associated with all their leaders and bold fellows,
and then led his companions
(Cáo means 'group' or 'generation')
to Fānyáng. The magistrate of Fānyáng, Wú Ruì,
was very popular among the people of the rivers and lakes region,
and was called Lord of Fān.
Bu went to see him,
his followers already numbering several thousand.
Lord Fān then gave him his daughter in marriage
and had him lead troops to attack Qin.
10 King Jǐng Jū of Chǔ was at Liú.
According to Bān's treatise,
Liú County belonged to the state of Chǔ.
The *Kuòdìzhì* states: Liú City is located 50 *lǐ* southeast of Pèi County in Xú Prefecture,
which is where Zhāng Liáng was enfeoffed.
Zhāng Liáng also gathered over a hundred young men intending to go and join Jǐng Jū.
On the road he met the Lord of Pèi,
and subsequently attached himself to him;
the Lord of Pèi appointed Liáng as a *jì* general.
A *jì* general likely oversaw horses.
The Lord of Pèi thought well of him
and often used his strategies;
when Liáng spoke to others,
none would heed him.
Liáng said:
"The Lord of Pèi is perhaps Heaven-sent!"
Therefore he stayed and did not leave.
This marks the beginning of Zhāng Liáng following the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi and Liáng together went to see Jǐng Jū,
wishing to request troops to attack Fēng.
At that time, Zhāng Hán's commander Sìmǎ was leading troops north to pacify the Chǔ territory,
(Yánzhī said: ,
the ancient character for 'Yí'. The *Lèipiān* says: the ancient character for 'Rén';
also pronounced Yánzhī.)
reaching Dàng.
According to Bān's treatise,
Xiàng County was the seat of Pèi Commandery.
The *Kuòdìzhì* states: The old Xiàng city
is located 90 *lǐ* west of Fúlí County in Xú Prefecture.
(Xiàng,
pronounced Xiàng. Dàng,
pronounced Dàng.)
They fought west of Xiāo.
According to Bān's treatise,
Xiāo County belonged to Pèi Commandery;
under Táng it belonged to Xú Prefecture.
'West of Xiāo' means west of Xiāo County.
They returned,
gathered troops, and assembled at Liú.
In the second month,
they attacked Dàng,
and in three days,
captured it;
they gathered troops from Dàng, obtaining six thousand men,
which combined with the former troops made nine thousand.
In the third month,
they attacked Xiàyì,
and captured it;
(According to Bān's treatise,
Xiàyì County belonged to the state of Liáng.)
but Fēng did not fall.
11 Zhào Píng of Guǎnglíng, acting on behalf of King Chén, was pacifying Guǎnglíng,
but had not yet captured it.

(Guǎnglíng County belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery. According to Bān's treatise it was the capital of the Kingdom of Guǎnglíng; under Táng it was Yáng Prefecture. The *Xìngpǔ* states: The Zhào surname descends from Shào Gōng Shì, son of King Wén of Zhōu. Zhào, pronounced Shào.)
Zhāng Hán was about to arrive,
so he crossed the river,
forged an order from King Chén,
and appointed Xiàng Liáng as Chǔ's Shàngzhùguó,
saying:
"Jiāngdōng is already pacified,
quickly lead troops west to attack Qin!"
Liáng then crossed the river with eight thousand men and headed west.
Hearing that Chén Yīng had already taken Dōngyáng,
(According to Bān's treatise,
Dōngyáng County belonged to Línhuái Commandery;
Emperor Míng divided it to belong to Xiàpī;
later it was again divided to belong to Guǎnglíng. The *Kuòdìzhì* states: The old city of Dōngyáng
is located 70 *lǐ* east of Xūyí County in Chǔ Prefecture. The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* says: Huáiyīn County
was Dōngyáng Commandery between the times of Chǔ and Hàn.)
Chén Yīng was formerly a clerk under the magistrate of Dōngyáng.

(Sū Lín said: A clerk is an office clerk. Jìn Zhuó said: According to the *Hàn Yí Zhù*, a magistrate's clerk is called a magistrate's clerk, a deputy's clerk is called a deputy's clerk. Yánzhī said: Jìn's explanation is correct.)
He was always trustworthy and cautious,
and was considered an elder.
The young men of Dōngyáng killed their magistrate,
gathered a force of twenty thousand men,
and wanted to make Yīng king.
Yīng's mother said to Yīng:
"Since I became a wife in your family,
I have never heard of any noble ancestors in your lineage.
Now suddenly gaining great fame
is inauspicious;
it would be better to attach yourself to someone.
If the undertaking succeeds,
you may still be enfeoffed as a marquis;
if it fails,
it will be easier to flee,
as you will not be a named target for the world."
Yīng then did not dare to become king,
and said to his military officers:
"The Xiàng family for generations have been a military family,
famous in Chǔ;
now if we want to undertake a great enterprise,
it will not succeed without the right leader.
If we rely on a famous clan,
the fall of Qin is certain!"
His followers obeyed him,
and he then placed his troops under Liáng's command.
Yīng Bu, having defeated the Qin army,
led his troops east;
hearing that Xiàng Liáng had crossed the Huái River westwards,
Bu and General Pú both placed their troops under his command.
Xiàng Liáng's forces totaled about sixty to seventy thousand men,
and they encamped at Xiàpī.
(According to Bān's treatise,

Xiàpī County belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery. Yīng Shào said: Pī was at Xuē, later it moved here, hence called Xiàpī. Chén Zàn said: There was an upper Pī, hence called lower Pī. The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* says: Xiàpī is Sìshuǐ County.)
Jǐng Jū and Qín Jiā's army was east of Péngchéng,
intending to block Liáng.
Liáng said to his military officers:
"King Chén was the first to initiate the uprising,
his battles were not successful,
and his whereabouts are unknown.
Now Qín Jiā has betrayed King Chén and set up Jǐng Jū,
a great act of treason and immorality!"
He then advanced his troops to attack Qín Jiā.
Qín Jiā's army was defeated and fled.
They pursued him
to Húlíng.
(Húlíng is Húlù. According to Bān's treatise it belonged to Shānyáng Commandery; Emperor Zhāng of Hàn changed it to Húlíng.)
After one day,
Jiā died,
and his army surrendered;
Jǐng Jū fled and died in Liáng territory.
(Liáng territory was the former territory of Wèi.)
Liáng, having absorbed Qín Jiā's army,
encamped at Húlíng,
then gathered his army and headed west.
Zhāng Hán's army reached Lì.
(According to Bān's treatise,
Lì County belonged to Pèi Commandery.)
Yú Fán Jūn died;
Zhū Jīshí's army was defeated,
and he fled to Húlíng.
Liáng then led his troops into Xuē
and executed Zhū Jīshí.
(The *Kuòdìzhì* says: The old Xuē city was the ancient state of Marquis Xuē, located within the boundaries of present-day Téng County in Xú Prefecture.)
The Lord of Pèi went with over a hundred cavalry to see Liáng;
Liáng gave the Lord of Pèi five thousand soldiers
and ten Wǔdàfū-ranked generals.
The Lord of Pèi returned,
led his troops to attack Fēng,
and captured it.
Yōng Chǐ fled to Wèi.
Xiang Liang sent Xiang Yu to attack Xiangcheng separately.
According to the Ban Zhi,
Xiangcheng County belonged to Yingchuan Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: It is present-day Xǔzhōu County.
After it was captured,
all were buried alive,
and he returned to report.
When Xiang Liang heard that King Chén had definitely died,
he summoned the various separate commanders to meet at Xuē to discuss matters.
The Lord of Pei also went there.
Fàn Zēng of Jūcháo,
seventy years old,
according to the Ban Zhi,
Jūcháo County belonged to Lújiāng Commandery.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals,
"The people of Chǔ besieged Cháo."
Cháo
was a state.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: It was the place where Xià Jié fled.
Jìn Zhuó said: Cháo
is pronounced like the "jiǎo" in "jiǎojué."
Shī Gǔ pronounces it as "cháo."
He was fond of ingenious strategies,
and went to persuade Xiang Liang, saying:
"Chén Shèng's defeat
was indeed fitting.
When Qín destroyed the six states,
Chǔ was the most blameless.
Since King Huái entered Qín and did not return,
the people of Chǔ pitied him.
This event is recorded in the fourth year of King Nǎn of Zhōu.
This should belong to the previous sentence.
'The one to destroy Qín must be Chǔ.'
Fú Qián said: Nán Gōng
was an elder of the south.
Yú Xǐ's Zhìlín states: Nán Gōng
was a Daoist,
who understood the patterns of rise and fall,
and knew that the one to destroy Qín must be Chǔ.
The Hànshū Yìwénzhì records: Nán Gōng in thirteen chapters,
a person from the Warring States period,
belonging to the Yin-Yang school.
Chén Zàn said: The people of Chǔ resented Qín,
even three households would be enough to destroy Qín.
Not establishing a descendant of Chǔ but proclaiming himself,
his position would not last long.
Now you have risen in Jiāngdōng,
and the generals who rose in Chǔ are all vying to join you because
Shī Gǔ said: Fēng
is the ancient character for "bee";
qǐ
is like the rising of bees,
meaning they are numerous.
Another interpretation: Fēng
is the same as "sharp,"
meaning those who rise sharply.
Ěryǎ Yì states: Fēng
is near its hive,
and they immediately rise up to attack people,
hence "generals who rise like bees."
It is because you can reestablish a descendant of Chǔ."
Thereupon, Xiang Liang agreed with his words,
and sought and found King Huái of Chǔ's grandson, Xīn, among the common people,
who was herding sheep.
In summer,
the sixth month,
he was established as King Huái of Chǔ,
following the people's hopes.
Xú Guǎng said: Complying with the people's hopes,
using his ancestor's posthumous title as his name.
He was enfeoffed with five counties,
and with King Huái, he made Xūyí the capital.
According to the Ban Zhi,
Xūyí County belonged to Línhuái Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: It is present-day Chǔzhōu County.
Ruǎn Shèngzhī's Nányǎnzhōu Jì states: Xūyí
was originally the land of Shàndào in the Spring and Autumn period;
during Sòng, it belonged to Sìzhōu.
Pronounced "Xūyí."
Zhāng Liáng persuaded Xiang Liang, saying:
"You have already established a descendant of Chǔ,
and among the various princes of Hán, Héngyáng Jūn Chéng is the most worthy.
He can be established as king,
to increase our allies."
Xiang Liang sent Zhāng Liáng to seek Hán Chéng,
and established him as King of Hán.
He appointed Zhāng Liáng as Sītú,
and with the King of Hán, led over a thousand men westward to seize Hán territory.
They captured several cities,
but Qín repeatedly retook them;
they moved back and forth as guerrilla troops in Yǐngchuān.
Yǐngchuān,
originally Hán territory,
was established as a commandery by Qín.
Chapter 12: Zhāng Hán had already defeated King Chén,
and then advanced his troops to attack the King of Wèi at Línjì.
According to the Hòu Hànzhì,
Píngqiū County in Chénliú Commandery had the Línjì Pavilion.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: It was where Tián Dān died.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: It is present-day Línjì County in Qízhōu.
It also says: The old city is two lǐ north of Gāoyuàn County in Zīzhōu.
I note that the Línjì mentioned in the Zhèngyì
is the land of Dí County where Tián Dān rose,
not the Línjì where King Jiù of Wèi resided.
The Hòu Hànzhì and Shuǐjīng Zhù are correct.
He sought aid from Qí and Chǔ;
the King of Qí, Tián Dān, and the Chǔ general Xiàng Tuō both led troops with Shì to rescue Wèi.
Zhāng Hán attacked at night with gagged troops,
and heavily defeated the Qí and Chǔ armies below Línjì.
Shī Gǔ said: Gagging means
stopping speech and clamor,
wanting the enemy not to know of their arrival.
The Zhōuguān has the position of Xiánméi Shì.
The gag is shaped like a chopstick,
held horizontally in the mouth,
tied around the neck.
Tying it
means to hinder,
wrapping means to bind,
probably tying a knot and wrapping it around the neck.
Xián
is pronounced "hù jiān fān."
Huò
is pronounced "huò."
Jié
is pronounced "jié."
King Jiù of Wèi made a surrender agreement with his people;
after the agreement was settled,
he burned himself to death.
His younger brother, Bào, fled to Chǔ.
King Huái of Chǔ gave Wèi Bào several thousand men,
and he again marched through Wèi territory.
Tián Róng of Qí gathered the remaining troops of his elder brother, Tián Dān,
and fled east to Dōng'ē.
According to the Ban Zhi,
Dōng'ē County belonged to Dōng Commandery.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Dōng'ē
is twenty-five lǐ southwest of Dōng'ē County in Jìzhōu.
The people of Qí, hearing of Tián Dān's death,
then established the younger brother of the former King Jiàn of Qí, Jiǎ, as king,
with Tián Jiǎo as chancellor,
and Jiǎo's younger brother, Jiān, as general,
to resist the various lords.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
there was heavy continuous rain.
Rain lasting three days or more is called "lín."
Hearing of Tián Róng's urgent situation,
he then led troops to attack and defeat Zhāng Hán's army below Dōng'ē;
Zhāng Hán fled westward.
Tián Róng led his troops east back to Qí.
Wǔxìn Jūn alone pursued the fleeing enemy,
sending Xiàng Yǔ and the Lord of Pei to attack Chéngyáng separately,
and massacred it.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Léizé County in Púzhōu
was originally Hàn's Chéngyáng,
located ninety-one lǐ east of the prefecture.
I note that according to the Ban Zhi,
Chéngyáng County in Jìyīn had Léizé.
This Chéngyáng is close to Dìngtáo and Púyáng,
not the Chéngyáng of the Chéngyáng Kingdom.
According to the Ban Zhi,
Púyáng County belonged to Dōng Commandery.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Púyáng County is eighty-six lǐ west of Púzhōu.
Pú
is pronounced "bǔ."
They again defeated them.
Zhāng Hán regained strength,
Lǐ Qí said: Zhèn
means to reorganize.
Rú Chún said: Zhèn
means to rise;
gathering scattered troops,
rising swiftly on one's own.
He encircled himself with water.
Wén Yǐng said: Diverting water to encircle and defend oneself firmly.
Huán
is pronounced "huàn."
He attacked Dìngtáo.
In the eighth month,
Tián Róng attacked and drove out King Jiǎ of Qí,
and Jiǎ fled to Chǔ.
Tián Jiān had earlier gone to rescue Zhào,
and thus stayed there, not daring to return.
Tián Róng then established Tián Dān's son, Shì, as King of Qí,
with Róng as his chancellor.
Tián Héng served as general,
pacifying Qí territory.
Zhāng Hán's troops grew stronger,
and Xiang Liang repeatedly sent messengers to urge Qí and Zhào to send troops to jointly attack Zhāng Hán.
Tián Róng said:
"If Chǔ kills Tián Jiǎo,
and Zhào kills Jiǎo and Jiān,
then I will send troops."
Chǔ and Zhào did not agree.
Tián Róng was angry,
and ultimately refused to send troops.
13 The Commandant of the Palace Guard, Zhào Gāo
Bān Biǎo states: The Commandant of the Palace Guard,
was an office of the Qín dynasty,
responsible for guarding the gates of the palace and its side entrances.
Chén Zàn said: He was in charge of the various officials within the guard,
hence called the Commandant of the Palace Guard;
Emperor Wǔ changed the title to Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
Because of personal grudges, he had killed many people;
fearing that the high officials would speak of this when they came to court to present affairs,
he then advised the Second Emperor, saying:
"The reason why the Son of Heaven is esteemed,
is solely because he is heard but not seen,
so that his ministers cannot see his face.
Moreover, Your Majesty is rich in years,
meaning young,
this says the years are many.
Now if you sit in court,
and any reprimands or promotions are inappropriate,
then your shortcomings will be exposed to the high officials,
which is not the way to display divine intelligence to the world.
Your Majesty would do better to remain deep within the forbidden palace,
Cài Yì said: Originally called the forbidden palace,
because the gates had restrictions,
and those not among the attending and serving officials could not casually enter;
the path where the leopard-tail banners were carried was also called the forbidden palace.
When matters arise, there will be means to handle them.
In this way,
then the high officials will not dare to present doubtful affairs,
and the world will praise you as a sage ruler."
The Second Emperor adopted his plan,
and thus did not sit in court to see the high officials,
but constantly stayed within the forbidden palace;
Zhào Gāo, as Palace Attendant, managed affairs.
Bān Biǎo states: Under the Qín system: Palace Attendant, Left and Right Officials, Various Clerks, Cavalier Attendants, and Regular Palace Attendants were all additional offices,
those appointed could be marquises, ministers, grandees, generals, commanders, commandants, masters of writing, imperial physicians, or masters of the imperial kitchen,
down to palace guards without fixed numbers,
sometimes as many as several tens of people;
Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants could enter the forbidden palace.
Yìng Shào said: They entered to attend the Son of Heaven,
hence called Palace Attendants.
The Later Hàn Records state: Palace Attendant,
rank equivalent to two thousand shi,
responsible for attending at the left and right,
assisting and guiding in various affairs,
advising and responding to inquiries.
Gāo heard that Lǐ Sī had spoken about this,
and then went to see the Chancellor, saying:
"The bandits east of the pass are many,
and now the Emperor is urgently increasing conscript labor,
to build the Ēpáng Palace,
gathering useless things like dogs and horses.
I wish to remonstrate,
but my position is lowly,
this is truly a matter for you, my lord;
why do you not remonstrate?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"Indeed,
I have long wished to speak of it.
But now the Emperor does not sit in court,
and constantly stays deep in the palace.
What I have to say,
cannot be transmitted;
I wish to see him,
but there is no opportunity."
Zhào Gāo said:
"If you truly can remonstrate,
allow me to wait for an opportunity when the Emperor is free,
and inform you."
Thereupon, Zhào Gāo, while attending
the Second Emperor who was feasting and enjoying himself,
with women before him,
sent someone to inform the Chancellor:
"The Emperor is free now,
you may present affairs."
The Chancellor came to the palace gate and requested an audience.
This happened three times.
The Second Emperor became angry, saying:
"I often have many free days,
and the Chancellor does not come;
when I am feasting privately,
the Chancellor then comes to request affairs!
Does the Chancellor perhaps look down on me,
or think me ignorant?"
"Look down on me"
means to despise me as young and immature.
"Think me ignorant"
means to despise me as ignorant and shallow.
"Now, the plot at Shāqiū,
the Chancellor participated in it.
The affair is seen in the previous volume, the thirty-seventh year of the First Emperor.
"Participated"
is read as "pre-".
Yet the Chancellor's nobility has not increased,
this shows his intention is also to hope for a fief and to become king.
Moreover, if Your Majesty did not ask me,
I would not dare speak.
The Chancellor's eldest son, Lǐ Yóu, is Governor of Sānchuān,
and the Chǔ bandits Chén Shèng and others are all sons of counties adjacent to the Chancellor's.
"Adjacent counties,"
means nearby counties.
Lǐ Sī
was from Shàngcài in Rǔnán;
Chén Shèng,
from Yángchéng in Yǐngchuān: Rǔnán and Yǐngchuān are close.
When they passed by Sānchuān city,
the governor
refused to attack.
I have heard that documents passed between them,
but have not obtained the details,
so I did not dare to inform you.
Moreover, the Chancellor resides outside,
and his power is greater than Your Majesty's."
The Second Emperor thought this correct,
and wished to investigate the Chancellor;
fearing the details were not clear,
he first sent someone to interrogate and verify the circumstances of the Governor of Sānchuān's communication with the bandits.
Lǐ Sī heard of this,
and accordingly submitted a memorial speaking of Zhào Gāo's faults, saying:
"Gāo is covetous of profit and fearful of harm,
no different from Your Majesty.
In the past, Tián Cháng served as Chancellor to Duke Jiǎn of Qí,
secretly appropriating his grace and authority,
gaining the common people below,
and the various ministers above,
and finally assassinated Duke Jiǎn and took the state of Qí,
the affair is seen in the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
"Finally,"
read as zú.
Now Gāo has treacherous and unrestrained ambitions,
dangerous and rebellious conduct,
and the wealth of his private household,
is like that of the Tián clan in Qí,
and moreover, his greed and desires are insatiable,
seeking profit without cease,
his position and power are second only to the ruler,
meaning Zhào Gāo, being at the center managing affairs,
his positional rank and power are second only to the ruler.
He seizes Your Majesty's authority and trust,
his ambition is like Hán Yí who became Chancellor to King Ān of Hán.
Suǒyǐn says:
"Yí,"
in one version is
"Qǐ,"
both pronounced yí,
a grandee of Hán,
who assassinated his ruler, Duke Dào.
However, Hán had no Duke Dào,
perhaps it refers to a successor ruler of Zhèng.
According to the tables: Hán Yí served Marquis Zhāo,
from Marquis Zhāo down four generations to King Ān,
this explanation is incorrect.
I observe the meaning of Lǐ Sī's letter,
precisely because the disaster of Húhài's loss of the state was imminent,
so he pointed to King Ān of Hán, using his employment of Hán Yí and the consequent loss of Hán to warn and move him.
In the time of King Ān of Hán,
among his ministers there certainly was a Hán Yí,
only the history has lost the details of the affair.
Lǐ Sī was contemporary with King Ān of Hán,
and the affair of King Ān's loss of his state was recent to Húhài's ears and eyes,
what is called
"the example of Yīn is not far."
Suǒyǐn, several hundred years later, argues that this explanation is incorrect,
how can that be!
"Trust,"
read as "extend."
I fear he will certainly rebel."
The Second Emperor said:
"What is this!
Now Gāo,
is originally a palace eunuch;
yet he does not indulge his will in times of peace,
nor change his heart in times of danger,
pure in conduct and cultivating goodness,
he has reached this position by his own efforts,
advanced through loyalty,
and maintains his position through trustworthiness,
I truly consider him worthy;
it is said that a ruler facing disorder,
each esteems his own ministers.
"Conduct,"
read as xìng.
Why?
Moreover, if I do not entrust matters to Lord Zhào,
then whom should I employ!
And Lord Zhào's character,
is astute, incorruptible, and strong in ability,
he understands human feelings below,
and above, he can accommodate me;
do not doubt him!"
The Second Emperor deeply loved Zhào
Gāo,
and fearing Lǐ Sī would kill him,
he privately informed Zhào Gāo.
Gāo said:
"The Chancellor's only worry is me;
if I die,
the Chancellor will then wish to do as Tián Cháng did."
At this time,
bandits and rebels grew ever more numerous,
and the troops from Guānzhōng sent east to attack the rebels were endless.
Right Chancellor Féng Qùjí, Left Chancellor Lǐ Sī, and General Féng Jié remonstrated, saying:
"Bandits and rebels in the lands east of the pass have risen together.
Qín has dispatched troops to punish
and attack them,
and those killed or lost are very many,
yet they still do not cease.
The bandits are numerous
all because garrison duty, water transport, land transport, and labor service are bitter.
'Shù'
means military conscription and garrison duty;
'cáo',
means water transport;
'zhuǎn',
means land transport;
'zuò',
means labor service.
'Shì kǔ'
means that these affairs are toilsome and bitter.
We request that the work on the Ēpáng Palace be temporarily halted,
and that garrison duties and transport on the four borders be reduced and curtailed."
The Second Emperor said:
"In general, the reason for valuing possession of the empire
is to be able to indulge one's will and exhaust one's desires,
and for the ruler to emphasize and clarify the laws.
This refers to the relationship between ruler and minister.
If what the superior emphasizes is weighty, then the influence of the inferior is light.
'Zhǔ zhòng'
is like saying 'to occupy a weighty position'.
'Zhòng'
is read as its usual pronunciation;
Kǎng reads it as 'zhí lóng qiè',
which is incorrect.
In this way, one can control and govern the Four Seas.
The rulers of Yú and Xià,
though noble as the Son of Heaven,
personally endured the reality of poverty and hardship for the sake of the common people—
what use did they have for laws!
This means, what affairs did they have for laws?
'Chǔ'
is read as 'chāng lǚ fān'.
Having unified All-under-Heaven,
and with All-under-Heaven already settled,
we drove back the Four Barbarians abroad to pacify the borders,
and built palaces and halls to manifest our satisfaction.
And you, my lords, have witnessed the achievements and legacy of the Former Emperor.
Now that We have ascended the throne,
within two years,
bandits and rebels have risen together.
You, my lords, have been unable to stop them,
and now you wish to abolish what the Former Emperor accomplished.
This shows that above, you have no way to repay the Former Emperor,
and next, you do not exert your utmost loyalty and strength for Us.
On what grounds do you remain in your positions!"
He dismissed Qùjí, Sī, and Jié from their posts and handed them over to the law officials,
investigating and charging them with other crimes.
Qùjí and Jié committed suicide;
only Lǐ Sī was sent to prison.
The Second Emperor entrusted Zhào Gāo to try him,
charging Sī with conspiring with his son Yóu to rebel.
All their clans and retainers were arrested.
Zhào Gāo tried Sī,
beating him over a thousand times.
Unable to bear the pain,
Sī falsely confessed.
He falsely accused himself of rebellion and admitted his guilt.
'Shèng'
is pronounced 'shēng'.
The reason Sī did not die
was that he relied on his own eloquence,
his achievements,
and the fact that he truly had no rebellious intent.
He wished to submit a memorial to explain himself,
hoping the Second Emperor would realize the truth and pardon him.
So he submitted a memorial from prison, saying:
"I have served as Chancellor governing the people
for over thirty years.
Reaching back to when the lands of Qín were narrow and confined,
they did not exceed a thousand lǐ,
with troops numbering several hundred thousand.
I exhausted my meager talents,
secretly employing strategists,
supplying them with gold and jade,
sending them to persuade the various feudal lords;
secretly cultivating armor and weapons,
rectifying governance and instruction,
promoting warriors to office,
and honoring meritorious ministers.
Therefore, we finally coerced Hán,
weakened Wèi,
crushed Yān and Zhào,
leveled Qí and Chǔ,
and ultimately unified the Six States,
capturing their kings,
and establishing Qín as the Son of Heaven.
Furthermore, we drove back the Hú and Mò in the north,
pacified the Bǎiyuè in the south,
to demonstrate Qín's strength.
We also reformed and standardized peck measures, dou and hu measures, weights and measures, and written characters,
promulgating them throughout the empire,
to establish Qín's name.
All these are my crimes,
and I should have died long ago!
Fortunately, the Emperor allowed me to exhaust my abilities,
so I have survived until now.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this!"
When the memorial was submitted,
Zhào Gāo had the clerks discard it and not present it,
saying:
"How can a prisoner submit a memorial!"
Zhào Gāo sent over ten of his retainers to pretend to be Imperial Secretaries, Messengers, and Palace Attendants,
taking turns to interrogate Sī again.
The title of Imperial Secretary
existed among the Zhōu officials;
the Warring States also had Imperial Secretaries.
At the meeting at Miǎnchí between Qín and Zhào,
each ordered them to record the proceedings,
so they were all positions responsible for recording events;
by Qín and Hàn times, they held investigative duties.
'Gèng'
means alternately.
'Fù'
means to review.
'Xùn'
means to question.
'Gèng'
is pronounced 'gōng héng fān'.
Each time, they had people beat him again.
Later, when the Second Emperor sent someone to verify Sī's case,
Sī, thinking it was like before,
ultimately did not dare to change his statement.
He admitted his guilt in his testimony,
and the verdict was submitted to the Emperor.
'Zòu dāng' means
when the case is complete, the verdict and proposed punishment are submitted.
Lù Wēnshū of Hàn said: Once the verdict is submitted,
even if Gāoyáo heard it,
he would still think death insufficient for the crime.
'Shàng'
is pronounced 'shí zhǎng fān'.
"If not for you, Lord Zhào,
We would have been sold out by the Chancellor!"
By the time the envoy sent by the Second Emperor to investigate the Governor of Sānchuān, Yóu, arrived,
the Chǔ troops had already attacked and killed him.
When the envoy came,
it happened that the Chancellor had been handed over to the law officials.
Gāo fabricated rebellious statements for both to make them corroborate each other.
He then had Sī sentenced to suffer the Five Punishments.
The Bǎn Zhì records: According to Qín law: Those condemned to the extermination of three clans
are first tattooed, have their noses cut off, and their left and right feet chopped off,
then are beaten to death,
have their heads displayed on poles,
and their flesh and bones minced in the market;
those guilty of slander or cursing
first have their tongues cut out: this is called undergoing the Five Punishments.
When Sī was taken out of prison,
he was bound together with his middle son.
Looking at his middle son, he said:
"I wish I could go with you again, leading the yellow dog,
and together go out the east gate of Shàngcài to chase crafty hares—
how could that be possible now!"
Then father and son wept together and were executed along with their three clans.
The Second Emperor then made Zhào Gāo Chancellor,
and all affairs, great and small, were decided by him.

and led his troops west,
then north
to Dìngtáo,

Xiàng Yǔ and Peì Gōng also fought the Qín army at Yōngqiū,

At that time, there was continuous rain,
from the seventh month to the ninth month.

Wàihuáng County belonged to Chénliú Commandery.

Kuòdìzhì: Chénliú,
a county of Biànzhōu,
fifty lǐ east of Zuǒzhōu.

Péngménjì: Péng Zǔ,

15 Wèi Bào captured over twenty cities of Wèi;

16 In the intercalary ninth month,
Wén Yǐng said: That is the intercalary ninth month.
At that time, the calendar system was abandoned,
and they did not know about intercalation,
hence it was called the later ninth month.
Rú Chún said: At that time, following Qín, they took the tenth month as the start of the year,
so by the ninth month, the year ended;
the later ninth month was the intercalary month.
Shī Gǔ said: Wén’s explanation is incorrect.
If the calendar system was abandoned and they did not know about intercalation,
then they should have simply called it the tenth month,
and there should not have been a later ninth month.
It seems that in the Qín calendar system,
intercalary months were always placed at the end of the year,
this idea likely came from the Zuǒzhuàn’s "returning the remainder to the end."
How can this be proven?
According to the Hàn tables and Shǐjì,
before the Hàn dynasty changed the Qín calendar,
up until Empress Gāo and Emperor Wén,
they repeatedly recorded a later ninth month;
this shows it was inherent,
not due to the calendar being abandoned.
Gòngfù said: I believe Yán’s explanation of the later ninth month is also incomplete.
If Qín knew about setting the calendar with intercalation,
why would they all consider it the ninth month?
It seems that Simǎ, when writing the Shǐjì,
since he referred to the Qín first month as the tenth month,
then referred to the intercalary month as the later ninth month.
This is how Simǎ narrated it,
not the Qín system.
He personally led it;
he made Pèi Gōng the chief of Dàng Commandery,
Sū Lín said: Chief,
is like a commandery governor.

he enfeoffed Xiàng Yǔ as Marquis of Cháng'ān,
with the title Lord of Lǔ;

Jùlù County belonged to Jùlù Commandery.

means a large forest.

being the supreme general,

changed to the departing tone,

Palace Counselor-in-Chief Zhào Gāo
(The Records of the Grand Historian:
After Lǐ Sī died,

feared that his ministers would not obey him,

He brought a deer and presented it to the Second Emperor, saying:

The Second Emperor laughed and said:
"Counselor-in-Chief, are you mistaken?
Calling a deer a horse?"
He asked his attendants.
Some remained silent,
some said it was a horse to flatter and comply with Zhào Gāo,
and some said it was a deer.
Gāo then secretly used the law to punish those who said it was a deer.
Afterwards, the ministers all feared Gāo,
and none dared speak of his faults.
Gāo had previously stated several times

The Second Emperor dreamed of a white tiger biting the left-side horse of his chariot,

Cān,

"The perimeter barracks have soldiers posted with great vigilance,

Wò,

Wéi,

They summoned the attendants;

Zhào Gāo then summoned all the senior officials and princes,

it is appropriate
to revert to the old title,

Zhào Gāo indeed went in person,

Yáo,

Kuài,

He heavily defeated them south of Lántián.
